speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your great generosity this morning. We will make sure that we do not abuse it. I also thank you for giving me the opportunity to continue my speech which was interrupted yesterday on the second reading debate on Bill C-124. As I said yesterday this bill amends the Currency Act and the amendments affect Part II of that Act which defines the investment powers of the Exchange Fund Account.
As I said yesterday as well the present act contains some restrictions on the maturity of securities issued by governments other than the U.S. government and by international organizations. With Bill C-124 these restrictions would be lifted so that securities issued by all governments, international organizations and institutions, as well as eligible government organizations, would be treated the same way as those issued by the American government are treated now. In this regard, let me point out that most investments by the Exchange Fund Account are denominated in currencies of industrial countries with the strongest economies such as the United States, Japan and Germany.
The amended act would allow the Exchange Fund Account to lend the securities it holds and to conclude repurchase agreements for these securities with the appropriate counterpart organizations.
The account would thus have more latitude in managing its assets. For example it could lend some of its securities instead of selling them in cases where the assets must be quickly converted into cash for intervention in the currency market.
Finally the Exchange Fund Account will be authorized to conclude agreements involving products derived from securities that it holds or may hold. This means that it can conclude option and futures agreements. The advantage is that these instruments, which are gaining importance on the major financial markets, can help increase revenue and spread the potential risks of fund assets.
In summary, the bill amending the Currency Act is essentially technical and seeks to update the investment authority of the Exchange Fund Account so as to increase the potential profitability of eligible assets held by the account. Furthermore, the bill does not change
Government Orders
the strict investment standards that now exist and are necessary for Canada's official currency reserves.
I believe that this bill deserves the support of hon. members and I ask all hon. members of this House for their support to pass this bill.
[English)

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the remarks of my friend opposite.
The government characterizes this particular bill as one of simple technical amendments. Unfortunately at this point in the debate and in the procedure I cannot agree it is merely simple technical amendments.
The bill purports to expand the powers of the Minister of Finance and his or her agent to deal with the assets and in the assets of Canada's exchange fund. The exchange fund is the pool of liquid currency and other liquid financial assets maintained by the Government of Canada to regulate and balance the value of the Canadian dollar abroad.
Most of Canada's foreign reserves, that is currencies of other nations that Canada's bank holds, are kept in the exchange fund. This bill purports to give to the minister a whole raft of new powers. Ordinarily one would not object to giving the minister the necessary powers that he or she needs to do the job, but here are some of the powers and some of the assets the Minister of Finance will be authorized to deal in.
In a moment or two I will go through the act as it is now just so we can see the difference. The act will permit the Minister of Finance to deal in and generally, to use the terms of the statute, to sell, lend, borrow or otherwise deal in currencies, units of accounts, gold deposits or securities, et cetera. That is a pretty wide definition.
Some of the financial instruments in which the minister will be authorized to deal include SDRs, deposit instruments authorized by the World Bank. Right now Canada holds foreign currencies of three foreign countries: the United States dollar, the German mark and the Japanese yen. Somewhere in history the pound sterling dropped out. In any event that is where we are now.
These powers would expand the ability of the Minister of Finance through the Bank of Canada or any agent. I

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
point out the agent in the act is simply not defined. The agent could be in law, based on what is here, the brother-in-law of the Minister of Finance. I am not saying that would ever happen. I am just saying the statute as it is now proposed does not define who the agent of the Minister of Finance may be.
Some of the other instruments include securities issued which in layman's terms may be stocks, shares or financial instruments issued by the government of another country or an agency or institution of any other country designated by the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance would first have to designate, and I will mention in a moment just what constraints there may be on the designation. That institution can be broadened to include any institution. There is no further definition.
Turning to the discretion of the minister to designate the country, the institution or the organization, the act says the minister may do any of the lending, borrowing or otherwise dealing in any of those financial instruments on any terms and conditions the minister thinks fit. There is no constraint on what the minister or his or her agent can deal with. That got the alarm bells ringing right away.
I want to compare what is here to the present act and the current provisions in the Currency Act which authorize the creation of the exchange fund and the acquisition of assets for the exchange fund for purposes, as I said, of keeping and securing our foreign exchange reserves. Those powers include, it should not surprise anyone, the ability to buy gold, the SDRs which are special bank deposits created and issued by World Bank organizations that are very safe, U.S. dollars and other "usable currencies".
At the moment the definition of which currencies may be used is the term freely usable currencies, and at the moment Canada only uses three: the U.S. dollar, the German mark and the Japanese yen. The minister in theory could purchase Russian roubles now if that were a freely usable currency, although right now from a practical point of view I am sure we would all agree that currency is not a freely usable currency. The minister would at least be constrained under the existing act.
Let us move to the present act. How would the minister be constrained? As I have just read, the minister under the new provisions would not be constrained at all because he or his agent may deal in any of these instruments or any currency for any country he or she thinks fit. There is no definition of the discretion, no limitation of the discretion.
The government has described the bill as being one that provides greater flexibility for the Minister of Finance. Given that there is no restriction put on the minister's discretion, I would have to agree it provides greater flexibility. In fact the sky is the limit.
Essentially the problem I have at the moment with the bill is that in return for the greater powers, the greater flexibility, there is no reciprocal increase in accountability to Parliament or the Canadian taxpayer. The same mechanism of accountability that existed previously will continue. That accountability involves a financial report on the exchange fund being prepared every year within five months following the end of the calendar year, that report being audited by the Auditor General of Canada, and that report and the audit being tabled in Parliament again within five months of the calendar year.
We have approximately at the greatest distance a 17-month time-lag between a transaction and the date when the bottom line is reported to Parliament. That is getting a little long in the tooth in terms of modem financial transactions.
I suggest even in that area there may well be room for more accountability to Parliament on the operations of the exchange fund, but that appears to be the extent that exists now. In return for the greater powers, greater flexibility, the sky is the limit in flexibility. There is no change in those accounting mechanisms to Parliament.
I know the provisions of this bill are proposed to this House in good faith. No one is trying to blind side the Canadian taxpayer. We have a ministry that is trying to get on with its job in a rapidly changing world. I guess that phrase is a bit of a cliche around here and probably in legislatures all around the world: Yes, do we have change for you.
The Department of Finance would be looking at of the financial transactions taking place globally, which transactions are now taking place 24 hours a day electronical-
May 11, 1993

Government Orders
ly. I guess the Bank of Canada traders will have to stay awake all night now. The Bank of Canada will need a night shift, and I suppose it does.
Between the time of hitting the sack and waking up in the morning you might have lost your shirt. Holding gold is one thing, but if you are holding one of these other instruments proposed in the new bill how do you know where you are going to end up the next day? Things can change overnight. The taxpayer, the owner of these assets, is therefore at risk.
We are not talking about conservative instruments like gold, gold certificates and U.S. currency. We are talking about something called futures, forward options, repurchase and reverse repurchase agreements, derivative or associated instruments or products. That covers a lot of territory. I have not even exhausted my imagination yet as to what those terms will comprehend, a derivative or associated instrument or product.
I am almost at the point of saying that pork bellies owned by a foreign country can be included in that definition. As long as it is designated, as long as the country is designated, as long as the issuer of the instrument, be that any unit or security invested in pork bellies, they have an investment in pork bellies. Now some people do quite well in commodities. I just do not think the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance need the authority to get into that play. Therefore I am very cautious.
Last week I gave a speech in Ottawa to the Canadian Institute for the Administration of Justice conference on legal drafting. I chair a parliamentary committee that spends almost all its time looking at the drafting of regulations trying to determine if the subsidiary laws, the subordinate laws that are the regulations made pursuant to statutes, are made within Canada's laws as enacted by Parliament. From time to time, believe it or not, we find laws that are not made within the ambit of the general law of Canada.
For the first time in Canadian history last year the committee disallowed a government regulation. It did not do it once; it did it three times. That was in the face of the refusal of the government to withdraw those regulations because we were of the view they did not comply with the law of Canada.
Speaking from that perspective, I gave a little speech and made light of how there was a trend in modem law making to give more and more powers to the Governor in Council or the executive branch of government. The tendency was to let the executive branch figure out the small details and make regulations governing what it does.
I told the true story of when a labour government was last elected in the United Kingdom. One prominent member of Parliament suggested publicly the government and Parliament should not get bogged down in fine details of legislation in Parliament, that they should simply pass a bill stating: "the Secretary of State may by regulation nationalize anything the Secretary of State sees fit".
That provoked a little bit of laughter at this event. It was a bit of a reach because the suggestion at that time was made in jest, but it was made in jest from an awareness that there is an increasing tendency to do it. We all had our little laugh at the expense of history.
The day before that event I was forwarded a copy of Bill C-124 which was introduced on April 21 last. Lo and behold, as I read clause 1(2) of this bill, keeping in mind what I just read about this suggestion in the United Kingdom, I read that the minister or an agent on behalf of the minister may sell, lend, borrow or otherwise deal in currencies, units of account, deposits, securities or notes, et cetera, on any terms and conditions the minister thinks fit. I suppose we were all laughing at what was taking place in our own backyards because that is exactly what this statute offers to the Canadian public, anything the minister sees fit.
In that same speech I made reference to a provision in a statute under the farm improvement and marketing co-operatives loans and fees regulations. Those regulations were made pursuant to a statute of this Parliament. In those regulations there is an authorization for the minister to deal with seized collateral that occurs after there is a material default in the loan of a borrower from the government backed financing of farms for the farming community.
I made note of the authority given to the minister to deal with this seized collateral, whether it be land, buildings, barns, farm machinery, banking assets, whatever is seized, whatever had been collateral, maybe even Canada Savings Bonds. In it the minister is authorized to

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
deal with any remaining security for the loan held by it in such a manner as the minister may direct. There is no other suggestion, no other reference in the regulations, as to what the minister should do with the seized collateral, these goods, these farms and farm machinery that have been owned by farmers, their whole livelihood.
At the time I said that kind of authority was the same as that given by King Richard to the sheriff of Nottingham in fictional days of yore. It was that kind of authority to do whatever the heck the sheriff wanted. That is the authority the Elouse gave to the minister under that act and that authority is exercised in such a manner as the minister may direct.
I am of the view that kind of authority given by the House is inappropriate. I realize the House would find it impossible to legislate what should happen with seized collateral in every different type of circumstance that could occur. However the regulations ought to be breaking down the scenarios and providing for certain procedures to be used when this collateral is disposed of.
In any event my purpose in raising that is not to deal with that particular set of regulations. It is to point out that this House has to be careful about the authority it delegates out of this House. When we give it, we give it on behalf of Canadian taxpayers. We cannot simply accept the wording and provisions put forward by officials in the Department of Finance. They have proposed here that the minister can designate whatever he or she wants and can deal in these items in whatever way he or she wants. I am sure most people would agree that is inappropriate.
I want to itemize for the record the concerns we have in relation to this statute. I know I could have read the bill in less time than it is taking me to talk about it. However I regard this as a veiy important issue. It is not the first and will not be the last time Parliament has had to deal with an issue like this one.
The first item is that clause 1(3) of the bill gives the Department of Finance infinitely more power than it has now. I say infinitely because there is no restraint whatsoever. The minister only has to designate. Those powers are not monitored at this time, not even under the current act, but at least we are only dealing with
overnight loans, some deposits, some stand-by lines of credit, gold, gold certificates and SDRs.
I should say that the people at the Bank of Canada want to be able to purchase and sell another unit. I have not mentioned it yet. It is the ECU, a financial instrument generated in the European Community. It is a solid, well backed currency and does not vary conceptually from the FDR. I agree our bank ought to be able to buy and sell ECUs as the need arises. At the moment it is not authorized to do that. However under the new act it certainly will be able to do that and more.
Perhaps it would have been easier had the bank and the ministry of finance simply recommended a specific list of things they wanted to do. Then we could have said yes or no. If they wanted to arrange for an expansion of the list then a regulation should have been provided that would authorize further expansion with notice to Parliament. They chose not to do that. They chose to use the constitutional counterpart of what is called the basket clause where everything, including the kitchen sink, is now included. That was one item.
There is no more monitoring of the bank as agent for the Minister of Finance than exists now, notwithstanding the desire to give it new powers.
An underlying problem we have is that guidelines currently exist for use by the Bank of Canada in investing our exchange fund and in dealing with our foreign reserves. That is what I am told. As I understand it, however, no one in this House other than the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance and perhaps the parliamentary secretary has seen those guidelines. I believe that is inappropriate, but that is another issue for another day.
The point I want to make is that the guidelines currently being used by which the Minister of Finance directs the Bank of Canada as his agent to deal in the exchange fund and in foreign reserves are not public. I have difficulty in giving more power or more authority to the Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Canada when we do not even know the rules under which they now operate.
I say this from the point of view of the taxpayer. I do not want them monkeying around any more. They have monkeyed around not too badly with the gold. I gather
May 11, 1993

we made a fair bit of money in liquidating some of our gold reserves but I am being very cautious. I have two examples which I will give later about why I am cautious.
Another point I want draw to the attention of the House is that at the moment when the minister decides he wants to use what is now called the freely usable currency, or in the future under this bill if it is passed a designation, there is no official mechanism for notifying the House or Canadians when a designation or a decision of that nature has been made. It simply does not show up on the Richter scale.
The bank publishes its annual report. If we read the report and if we see that the bank in its asset statement has invested in xyz instrument we can infer pretty easily that xyz instrument has been authorized. We may not know about it until a whole year has passed. I do not know whether it is appropriate for that degree of privacy inside the bank transactions to occur.
I accept the bank could not carry on its day-to-day business if it had reporters and parliamentarians looking over its shoulder. In order to carry out financial transactions in the medium and even in the short run, there must be a degree of confidentiality, and that is recognized around this House. It is certainly recognized when the government deals with financial and commercial institutions. There is such a thing as commercial confidentiality which is necessary.
Apparently last week word that the Government of Canada wanted to buy back some of its medium term bonds leaked out on the street. These bonds had sold at relatively high interest rates, the rates of three or four years ago. The government prudently wanted to buy them back and refinance at the current lower interest rate thereby saving the taxpayer a whole lot of dough. We do not know how word leaked out. Without the confidentiality, the price of those longer run bonds was bid up. If Canada had proceeded the bank would have had to buy those bonds back at the higher price. That is the price we have paid by the lack of confidentiality. I mention this simply to acknowledge that the bank requires a degree of confidentiality and privacy when it carries on its work.
I want to say that over all we require a bit more disclosure, maybe a lot more disclosure, from the bank and from the Minister of Finance on how the bank and the ministry conduct their affairs in these markets. I suggest that one report per year is not adequate. There
Government Orders
should be more. I am sure that if those wizards over at the Bank of Canada, as many of them are, would put on their thinking caps, they would easily devise a mechanism to better inform Parliament of what they are doing.
I want to mention two scenarios and I take full responsibility for authorship. Any connection between any individual alive or dead is unintended. I do not suggest that anything like this has happened or will happen. These are hypothetical scenarios of what I think could happen under the provisions of the bill.
In the first scenario the Bank of Canada has indicated to the minister and the minister has indicated to me that the bank would like to be able to place, among other financial instruments, these foreign reserves into income yielding securities. Rather than having dollar bills sitting around in a vault it wants to invest in a security that will earn a small income. By the way, it has been indicated this could produce $10 million to $12 million income a year if the bank had these increased powers.
What is being proposed is the buying of an instrument which is like a bond. It is issued in the United States. It is a bond issued by a U.S. government agency to finance residential mortgages. I do not think we have anything like that here. Maybe we should.
They have become known as Fannie MAEs. These bonds are backed by the U.S. government. They are just about as secure as we can get. The yield, the interest rate paid, the coupon rate, is not half bad. It is not great, but it is better than a lot of other things. Therefore the bank wants to be able to buy some of them from time to time. Under this bill those Fannie MAEs would have to be designated as an instrument and the United States would have to be designated as a country in whose currency those securities would have to be so we could buy them.
There is another provision in the bill which I have mentioned and that is called the derivative or associated instrument or product. Let us hypothesize that a mutual fund in Canada decides to invest exclusively in Fannie MAEs. What would happen is that unit of the mutual fund would then be, as I read it, a derivative or associated instrument.
It is then possible for the Minister of Finance to buy that associated instrument, that unit in the Canadian mutual fund investing exclusively in Fannie MAEs. I do not have any real problem with that until we start to

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
realize that the Minister of Finance is about to set up office on Bay Street. What happens when the hypothetical brother-in-law of the brother-in-law says: "I have a great rate on these Fannie MAEs. I have the ones you want. My commission rate is lower than you are going to get anywhere else"?
At this point we have a situation I think we would rather not have, of the minister being authorized to do whatever he thinks fit and being tempted to authorize or permit or simply acquiesce in his agent, the Bank of Canada, and of course there is not an institution or a man or woman in the Bank of Canada who has a brother-in-law who has just presented a great deal for the taxpayers being tempted to deal in a certain way with our foreign reserves. I do not think that clause ought to be there. That is scenario number one.
In the second scenario there is so much flexibility being offered to the Minister of Finance that there may be a temptation to have the Minister of Finance do political quid pro quo in the future. Here is the scenario.
The hypothetical Prime Minister of Canada visits the hypothetical country of Russia and the hypothetical president of Russia whose currency is roubles says: "You have to bail me out. I will do you a favour, Mr. hypothetical Prime Minister of Canada. I am prepared to send my armed forces to a hypothetical UN hot spot, no names mentioned. I can get them there within eight days. I can get this through my hypothetical parliament. I know you need the troops. I know you are having trouble there and these troops are exactly what you need for that hypothetical hot spot. But in return, Mr. hypothetical Prime Minister of Canada, you have to do me a favour. I have some problems in New York with the rouble. I want you and this hypothetical other country, or if I can get three other countries onside, to do a favour with the hypothetical rouble. Then we have a deal on the armed forces. You buy the rouble. You bail me out in New York and everybody is happy".
Then the hypothetical Prime Minister of Canada calls the hypothetical Minister of Finance and says: "Hypothetical Bob, you have to pick up these roubles through such-and-such a brokerage house on such-and-such a
day. It is a deal. Get the bank to do it". The Minister of Finance hypothetically designates the Russian rouble, may designate a derivative instrument and may authorize someone in the Bank of Canada to cut a deal with some brokerage house dealing with banks of other countries.
The deal is done; the money is invested. I do not care whether it is a purchase or repurchase, a lending or deposit, but the deal is done for an international political reason. It is not a selfish political reason necessarily but an international political reason. However the deal may be done to the great prejudice of Canada's foreign reserves.
Maybe the hypothetical Prime Minister thinks it is worth it in terms of international stability. Maybe those hypothetical foreign military forces would be just what the doctor needed to get a hypothetical international deal together, but the Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada are then authorized and would in that hypothetical situation be doing something we in the House would probably not otherwise authorize.
I want members on both sides to be aware of this particular problem, not the hypothetical one because as far as I know it has not happened and no one is planning to do it. Under these rules this is what is proposed.
Regrettably I cannot offer the support of my party at this time on such a small, easy technical amendment, as the government says. I cannot offer that support. This bill will clearly have to be looked at more closely at committee. A decision will be made at that time.
I encourage the government. I encourage the member opposite who led off the debate, the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization who proposed the bill and officials in the Bank of Canada to take a look at a couple of other sections of the Currency Act to see whether or not they can do better in the way they account to Parliament, to make Parliament feel that in return for this massive new authority to deal in financial assets there is a reciprocal giving back of accountability to Parliament and the people of Canada. I know there will be a way to do that because I have seen it happen in other ways around the House in the last three or four years. There is more than one way to skin a cat, and if there is goodwill on both sides I think that can be found.

Having said that, I encourage the government to respond before or after this bill gets to committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on behalf of our party about Bill C-124, an act to amend the Currency Act. It deals specifically with the exchange fund account that is part of the Currency Act.
I do not want to spend more than a few minutes on it this morning. I think the appropriate place to examine this bill is in the finance committee where we have a chance to call expert witnesses and put some very specific questions to them, be they from the Department of Finance or the Bank of Canada. I think that is the appropriate place to deal with it.
This bill is highly technical, dealing with the powers of the Minister of Finance concerning our exchange fund. In addition to being highly technical it is also a fairly sweeping bill in terms of the new powers the Minister of Finance will be given if Parliament approves the amendments to the Currency Act.
The Currency Act was first passed back in 1935. It was introduced to try to bring some stability to the Canadian currency at that time in terms of the ups and downs of the Canadian dollar. It dealt with foreign exchange and monetary items of that nature. The assets the exchange fund now deals with are primarily the American dollar, the German Deutschmark and the Japanese yen.
We in this House are being asked to provide the Minister of Finance with fairly sweeping new powers in terms of the exchange fund. For example, the minister could designate currencies other than the yen, the Deutschmark or the American dollar to be used in the exchange fund. He could designate the French franc, the British pound or whatnot as appropriate currencies for the fund.
The minister would also have other powers in addition to that, powers which would concern the units of the account to be designated by the minister, powers to deal in gold, to deal with a number of other deposits, to have a lot more flexibility in dealing with securities, and so on. In reality it would give a lot more power to the Minister of Finance to deal with the exchange rate and the exchange fund.
Government Orders
My main concerns are the ones I will now talk about. I ask these questions not in a critical nature but in the nature of trying to scrutinize whether or not these powers are necessary.
I would like the government to explain why it needs these additional powers given to the Minister of Finance, whoever it is in the future. When this Parliament passes this bill, as I assume we will, we will not really be giving the Minister of Finance from Vegreville these powers because in all likelihood he will not be the minister for very long. We will be giving these powers to future ministers of finance through the end of the century and into the next century.
First, I am not sure whether these powers are necessary. I know some of them probably are, but are we going too far? Is this really appropriate? These are the kinds of questions we should probably get answers to in committee.
Second, how do these changes compare to the laws of other countries around the world? How do they compare with the way that the Americans deal with this particular issue in terms of their exchange funds, or the British, French, Germans, Japanese or Scandinavians? Are these powers roughly similar to the powers in other countries?

It has changed radically over the last 10 years or 15 years in terms of globalization, the movement of currency around the world and the movement of stocks and bonds around the world, the liberalization of trade laws and so on. The government argues we have to update the Currency Act so that we have the same flexibility in our country through the Ministry of Finance.
Those may be and indeed are very appropriate arguments. The world has changed very rapidly, but are these the appropriate powers? That is the question we must have government officials respond to before the committee.
Another concern I have is whether these new powers given to the Minister of Finance will affect the relationship with the Bank of Canada. I would like to see the Governor of the Bank of Canada or the appropriate officials from the bank appear before the committee and tell us how they feel about these new powers being given to the Minister of Finance in the future. The relation-

How is that minister going to be accountable to Parliament for what is done?

Monetary policy affects not only the federal government but all the provinces and territories. I would like to know whether the Ministry of Finance has conducted the appropriate consultations with the provinces, with the various departments of finance across this country, to determine whether there is some input from the provinces that might be useful and whether the provinces agree with the proposed amendments before the House today.

We do not have to spend much time on second reading of this bill in the House. Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to lead off the debate on second reading of Bill C-122.
Bill C-122 is an important bill that will cause to come into force a number of tariff reductions announced by the government in its December economic and fiscal statement. The purpose of this bill is to implement tariff reductions on textile fibres, yarns and fabrics, effective January 1, 1993.
I will now touch briefly on the main factors that led to the drafting of Bill C-122.
In February 1989 the government asked the Canadian International Trade Tribunal to provide advice on the level and pace of textile tariff reductions that would be necessary to maintain the competitive position of the Canadian apparel industry and other downstream users of textile products. After a year of extensive public hearings on the matter, the tribunal recommended that a simpler tariff structure be adopted with maximum rates of 5 per cent for fibres, 10 per cent for yams and 16 per cent for fabrics. I may add that Canada's current rates
are, respectively, around 8 per cent, 13 per cent and 18 to 25 per cent.
The tribunal suggested that tariff rates on certain specially constructed textiles be reduced by one-third and that the complex, annually calculated rate on certain wool fabrics be fixed at 11.8 per cent. It also proposed that the reductions be phased in at a rate of one percentage point a year, once the results of the Uruguay Round of multilateral trade negotiations are known, but not later than 1991.
Under the tribunal's recommendations, Canadian textile tariffs will be reduced by an average of 26 per cent, leaving them, on average, slightly higher than those in the U.S. and substantially higher than those in the European Economic Community and Japan.
The tribunal concluded that its recommendations would provide overall net benefits to the Canadian economy, with only a relatively small impact on the textile industry.
The government expressed its agreement with the general tenor of these proposals when it announced that it would act on the tribunal's recommendations within the framework of decisions to be made in the course of the Uruguay round of multilateral trade negotiations. The textile and apparel industries have therefore started to make the appropriate adjustments with this in mind.
This bill contains legislative amendments to implement the tribunal's recommendations, effective January 1, 1993, with the following modifications.
First, to compensate for the delay in implementation, tariff reductions are being phased in at a rate of 1.5 per cent per year, rather than the 1 per cent recommended by the tribunal.
Second, to further simplify the tariff structure, all textile yams, fabrics and fibres are being treated the same. That is, tariffs on them are being reduced to maximum rates of 5 per cent, 10 per cent and 16 per cent, respectively, with no special treatment for specialty textiles or certain wool fabrics, as recommended by the tribunal.
Third, in accordance with our international obligations, margins of tariff preference are being maintained for Australia and New Zealand for six tariff items in which there is significant trade from these countries.
May 11, 1993

In a nutshell, Bill C-122 is important legislation that contains the long-awaited textile tariff reductions.
If adopted, the bill will have the effect of amending the Customs Tariff so as to implement textile tariff reductions effective January 1, 1993. The bill as such constitutes a fair and reasonable approach to the question of textile tariff reduction.
For years, Canadian textile tariffs have been significantly higher than those of other industrialized countries, and this has affected the international and national competitiveness of textile-using industries and increased costs to Canadian consumers. To help strengthen the competitive position of the Canadian apparel and textile industries, the government announced certain tariff relief measures in March 1988. The measures included a commitment to reduce textile tariffs to levels comparable with other industrialized countries, particularly the U.S., whose textile-using industries compete more directly with Canadian industries.
These tariff reductions will help gradually to lower the cost of production factors for the apparel industry and other downstream industries. At the same time, the Canadian textile industry would have only limited adjustments to make. Reducing textile tariffs is the best way to ensure that Canadian companies that use substantial quantities of textiles are able to compete on an equal footing with other companies, on the North American market and elsewhere. Reducing tariffs on textiles will lower costs for Canadian companies in the apparel industry, thus making them more competitive and able to market their products at prices that are more attractive to the consumer.
The textile tariff reductions are a constructive measure that will help improve the competitive position of the apparel industry and other textile-using industries in Canada, while having a limited impact on our domestic textile industry. Furthermore, these reductions are in line with the general free trade policy pursued by this government.
In response to comments by textile using industries, in 1988 the government announced its intention to proceed with textile tariff reductions. It then started extensive consultations to ensure that the interests of all parties would be considered.

To protect our competitive position, Canada must work to lower economic costs where possible. One way is by lowering tariffs on goods we import. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the bill this morning. I am not our party's critic in this area but unfortunately the member for Chambly is not here. He will be here after Question Period and will be speaking with a lot more detail concerning the bill than I will be this morning.
I want to talk for a few minutes about the impact of this bill. It is another piece of legislation that is really assisting to implement the free trade agreement and to anticipate the NAFTA with Mexico. We have already seen the devastation that has taken place in our industrial and manufacturing sectors with the free trade agreement.
A great deal of the clothing and textile industry is centred in the province of Quebec. The garment part of that industry employed 95,000 people in 1988. By 1992 employment had dropped to 62,000, a drop of one-third in the work force. Industry after industry reflects this right across the country.
As we look toward competing with Mexico we know that 87 per cent of our trade with Mexico is in imports to Canada from Mexico. Canada exports very little to Mexico in the way of hard consumer goods. That is quite logical if one thinks about it. Very few Mexicans are capable of purchasing Canadian made goods because they do not have the income. Only 10 per cent or about 8.5 million Mexicans have any capability of purchasing Canadian made goods or have the equivalent purchasing power of Canadians.
These pieces of legislation are basically setting us up to compete against low wages and low standards in Mexico. It is not possible to do so on an ongoing basis.
This legislation was supposed to assist by reducing certain tariffs over a period of time. However when one looks at it a lot of false premises were made in proposing this legislation. My understanding is the government made assumptions that Canadian textile tariffs were twice as high as the textile tariffs in other industrial countries including our major trading partner, the United States. That turned out to be not so. Therefore the whole notion of this bill, of unilateral tariff reduction, was based on a false premise.
It is also ironic that when the government is trying to negotiate agreements within bilateral trade agreements either through the Uruguay round at GATT or even in its wimpish way of trying to do it through the North American free trade agreement, the government unilaterally gives away its negotiating tools, its powers. Therefore the situation is that the government in the way it has been approaching trade with the United States is simply giving in before even being asked.
It is interesting the government has said during the Uruguay round that it will ensure the textile and clothing industry enjoys over-all protection equivalent to what is available for the major trading partners, but particularly the United States. This is not so because the apparel industry claims that the NAFTA rules of origin will prohibit them from taking advantage of free trade and that there is going to be an inundation of cheap Mexican clothing imports.
This whole notion we can enter into trade agreements on an equal basis would be fine if we were countries with equal footing. The areas I am concerned about are not only the cheap wages in Mexico but also the working conditions. Eighty-five per cent of the American companies now located in Mexico violate the Mexican law on environmental standards. Labour standards as to the age of working are not maintained. There are all sorts of examples in Mexico of children under the legal age for employment working and being exploited.
The government backs the reduction in wages and working conditions for ordinary workers. There has been a 60 per cent reduction in the actual wages of Mexicans in the last few years. There have been examples on the docks where workers actually won through free collective bargaining the right to reasonable and adequate

wages. The government came in and through legislation cut the wages to one-seventh of what had been won through free collective bargaining.
The fact that we continue our whole trade policy in looking toward Mexico is particularly galling to us in British Columbia. Fifty per cent of our trade right now is with the Pacific Rim, and there are far more trade opportunities in the Pacific Rim than there are for Canada going south to Mexico or to the United States. I will give a very concrete example.
A year ago I had the opportunity to travel to India. We were in an area in the Punjab not frequented by tourists. In the marketplaces I began to realize there were vast quantities of fairly expensive consumer goods, good quality electrical appliances, tremendous fabrics, clothing and all sorts of other traditional consumer goods. I tried to figure out who purchased them because my understanding of India was that it was a very poor, backward country.
I found out that in India there are 50 million very wealthy people. They are the old families, many of them landed class families. They are owners of manufacturing concerns and are exceptionally wealthy.
There are another 250 million middle class people living in India. These are the professionals, the more wealthy farmers, particularly in the Punjab and the more productive parts of India. They have buying power comparable to that of Canadians. There are 250 million of them.
Yes, there are 300 million poor in India. They have very little. Below those 300 million poor, there are 300 million who have nothing. The difference between being poor and having nothing in India may be as simple as having a blanket. The reality is that in India there is a pool of over 300 million people who have more consumer buying power or equivalent consumer buying power of Canadians.

I hear the member getting very excited. Since the free trade agreement was brought in 23 per cent of manufacturing jobs in this country have been lost. Does the member know that during the Great Depression we lost only 29 per cent of our manufacturing jobs?
It says it is because of the recession. During the same period the United States lost 6 per cent of its manufacturing jobs and we lost 23 per cent. Who got the best end of the deal? Even the Conservatives should begin to understand that if we lose 23 per cent of the manufacturing jobs, almost the same amount as in the Great Depression, we did not get a very good deal.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time has expired. This bill is an attempt to accelerate the kinds of
Last week in Toronto we lost for the first time ever a complete assembly plant. It was the Scarborough van plant; 3,500 skilled workers walked away from the plant last Thursday. On the previous Saturday they had a rally-I called it a funeral-to remind people of the community this was happening.
I must confess it was not until I saw the looks in the eyes of those men, women, husbands, wives and children at the plant that day and I listened to their feelings that I really understood how devastating it can be when an entire plant is shut down. It was an entire plant that in terms of spin-offs-in other words suppliers to the plant-might be affecting another 8,000 to 10,000 people who we do not see. They are nameless, but they are out there and they will be going on the long list of unemployed. Ultimately from unemployment insurance they move on to welfare.
May 11, 1993

In the face of what is happening in our country today, with the real lack of confidence and the real hopeless feeling that is out there, I do not know how the government can bring forward another bill that is undoubtedly going to lead to further plant shut downs or further plant closures.
The textile manufacturers or the people who are dealing in textile products in the province of Quebec must be scratching their heads when they see a bill like this one going through the House of Commons. When this kind of a mood is in the economy and the confidence level is so low, I do not know why the government would not say time out and let us go back to the drawing-board. That is the reasonable thing to do.
The government extended its mandate in terms of the election by a year. We should have had an election a year ago but it decided to take that extra year. That is fine. Constitutionally we realize and the people realize it has that right. However, during this period why would it not take the time to go back to the drawing-board with some of the obvious defects that are related to the free trade agreement?
There is absolutely no one on that side of the House who can say we would not make amendments to the free trade agreement. I defy one of them to stand and say: "We think all aspects of this free trade agreement are working well". They cannot say it because they know it is not working well. What would they rather do?
It seems to me that spending $200 million of taxpayers' money to do some retrofitting of the Scarborough van plant and allowing it to continue to operate versus spending $700 million the first year on unemployment insurance and welfare means that there is not much choice. I would go for the retrofitting of the van plant, which is the same thing we did in 1981 when we had a similar problem in terms of a deep recession and we had a choice. We spent, on behalf of the Canadian taxpayers, close to $800 million in the Brampton superplant and it became the envy of the world. Right now it is the anchor around which the Chrysler Corporation is manufacturing and exporting. That superplant in Brampton is one of the envies of the world. It was done through a decision taken
Government Orders
by the Government of Canada at the time and it was done with taxpayers' money, but we kept people working in the automotive parts business.
What has that to do with the bill on the floor of the House of Commons today? This is a further reduction of tariffs in the textile business. I just do not see the logic of where the government is coming from when we are competing against the Mexican market right now, when there is absolutely no focus on environmental standards and absolutely no focus on labour standards.
It is not just the Liberal Party of Canada saying this. The government likes to brag about its closeness with the United States government. Even the United States government right now is saying: "Time out on NAFTA until we look at the labour standards and at the environmental standards. There is no way the NAFTA is going through Congress until we have a handle on what is going on there and what it means in terms of all the manufacturing jobs that are directly or indirectly related in the United States". Why the government could not get a cue from that action is beyond me.
I have to say on behalf of my party that I am disturbed by the bill today because it is a symbol of what is happening across the country. It shows carelessness, a lack of sensitivity.
We have to start building hope and building confidence in the country. The government has a couple of things it can do quickly to get that hope and that confidence going. I refer specifically to the small business sector. I have deep respect for the Minister of Finance. I believed him when he said in mid-December in his economic statement that he was going to make sure financing for the small business sector would be looked after through the amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act.
We missed the January period to put the bill through because the House was adjourned. We understand that, but when we came back toward the end of the February the bill went through committee and the House inside of seven or eight days. However, one of the conditions that we attached to our total support for the bill was that the Government of Canada would make sure the the banks and financial institutions of Canada would co-operate and get behind the Small Businesses Loans Act.

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
You were sitting in the House of Commons during those debates, Mr. Speaker, and heard many members on that side of the House agree with us that this instrument was only going to work if the banks were part of the equation. I know the Bank of Nova Scotia took a small ad out in most of the newspapers of the country saying it was involved with the Small Businesses Loans Act, but day after day many members of our caucus are hearing from small businesses that say it is not working. The banks are not co-operating with the Small Businesses Loans Act.
For those who are not familiar with the Small Businesses Loans Act, it is an instrument that has been in existence for many years but the Minister of Finance amended it to make it much more meaningful for today's marketplace. If the owner of a business where the sales are $5 million or less wants to expand it with new technology or if someone wants to start a business, the Government of Canada will guarantee 90 per cent of a loan up to $250,000. The maximum rate is 1.75 per cent over prime.
The Minister of Finance focused on this area because he knows that the small business sector is where the new jobs are going to be created. The 1.3 million operating businesses out there are going to create some hope and opportunity when we are losing plants like General Motors and when textile operations are shutting down in south Toronto and different parts of Quebec.
We cannot just bring in a bill like this one and throw away all the safeguards as we define them without having the rest of the economic equation in place. The small business sector is one part of that economic equation that really must be in place, must feel confident and must be flowing, but it needs access to capital, to the banks of Canada, to the financial institutions of Canada.
I have repeated this message to the government no less than a dozen times in the last two months and it is still not playing ball. Who are the losers? The losers are not only our nation and the people within our nation but quite frankly the banks are losing too.
The banks are losing because all bank presidents three months ago in their annual report bragged about the fact they had to put something back into this recovery. They had to show they were committed to the new spirit, the
new economy, the new entrepreneurship that was developing. We know that unless that new entrepreneurship is functioning we are not going to be able to cope with the job losses that are inevitable with Bill C-122. It effectively reduces tariffs to the point where whole sectors of our economy are going to be boarded up and whitewashed.
Earlier today my colleague for Eglinton-Lawrence talked about for lease or for rent signs not by the dozens but by the hundreds and signs indicating rent free for three years. This has a compounded effect. It is like a brush fire. Today most people with jobs are as nervous or more nervous than the people without jobs. When they drive to work in the morning they see more for sale, for lease, or rent free for the next five years signs every day. This does not encourage the few consumers we have left to go out and buy, go out to restaurants or buy new cars, all the things we need to make our community function.
The government has made a bad mistake in the way it has ignored the whole aspect of adjustment. It moved forward on this flawed free trade agreement without any kind of adjustment process. I would even include in the notion of adjustment a terrific emphasis on a thrust from small business across the country. The fact that the government just talked about it but did not really make it happen is another example of a lack of sensitivity, connection, caring and compassion.
I know that after the next election-and we Liberals are not perfect- the greatest responsibility we are going to have is to put people back to work. When we look into the eyes of those people who lost their jobs at the Scarborough van plant last week, we have to remember the Scarborough van plant was a highly profitable company within the General Motors operation. The Minister for International Trade always likes to talk about global competitiveness and how we have to be lean, mean and globally competitive. This was an example of a company that won environmental standards and productivity awards. It made money for that transnational corporation General Motors and it still got the axe. It still got the knife.
Those people do not just fade away like the machinery that went on the trucks to Flint, Michigan. Those people are our constituents and there are people like that right across the country. It is going to be our responsibility
May 11, 1993

with all our imperfections to put them back to work after the next election.
The government would be doing something responsible if it withdrew the bill and let us go back to the drawing-board. Let us see what all the ramifications are as they relate to the NAFTA. When we see that General Motors in one year went from 6,000 to 60,000 people in Mexico there has to be a reason for it. When tariffs have been taken down in the textile industry we should not think the same thing is not going to happen in that sector. That is going to be the next sector to expand in Mexico. At whose expense? The people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my learned colleague has set out the problem for us quite clearly. All members on this side and I are as opposed to this NAFTA process as we were to the free trade deal. My colleague just mentioned that the jobs at General Motors went from 6,000 to 60,000 in one year in Mexico. I am from a riding where we have lost 8,000 jobs in General Motors. These were not just menial jobs. They were jobs for highly skilled machinists, tradesmen and electricians. To people who say they will find jobs elsewhere I say those jobs have gone south.
I would point out another thing my colleague probably already knows. It is a fact that today as I speak in this Flouse of Commons there are more General Motors workers in Mexico than there are in Canada. Why has there been this great shift and what has been the over-all effect? We who are close to the American border have felt the full brunt of this free trade deal that was supposed to give us access to the American market and did not. Now what are we told the North American free trade agreement is going to give us? More of the same.
Just the other evening the past Minister of Finance said he supported a candidate in the leadership race who was going to carry on the policies of this government which have proven in the last years to be bankrupt.
My hon. friend mentioned small businesses and the fact that the banks-he did not use this word but I will use it-are virtually raping the small businesses of this country. The loans they give them are usurious. They are
Government Orders
always sitting on top of them for proof that they do not need the money so they can give it to them.
My question for my hon. colleague is straightforward. What could we possibly do to ensure that our small businesses get a fair shake in this our beloved Canada?

Mr. Speaker, we can do a couple of things. First we passed a bill in the House about six months ago called the Bank Act. There was a Liberal amendment the government accepted that very few people in Canada know about.
The amendment indicates that if a small business feels it is not being treated fairly by its financial institution it has the right to call the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and give him the case and the reason it is not being treated fairly.
The Superintendent of Financial Institutions by the law of this land and this Parliament is bound to investigate that case. If the Superintendent of Financial Institutions finds that small business or individual is not being treated fairly, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions is by the law of this land bound to report that bank in the annual financial report of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
As long as the banks feel they can muscle small businesses and their customers they are going to continue to do whatever they want on their own terms. We have to give the people of Canada confidence that we respect the stability of the financial institutions. They are part of our community and as such have a responsibility to work with us and honour the laws of the land that have been made in this Parliament.
One of those laws that all parties agreed to in the last 90 days-they are not working under it yet-is the Small Businesses Loans Act. If a bank is not co-operating, call the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.

Mr. Speaker, I find my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood most stimulating in debate as usual. He raises some issues that are absolutely crucial to the well-being of this country. He pointed out that we have another 3,500 skilled, well paying jobs from a consolidated revenue perspective. These are jobs that generate much needed tax moneys for our beloved social programs.

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
I ask him and I ask myself what we do in the House when we consider legislative items like Bill C-122 that do not take into consideration the necessary safeguards when we establish an industrial policy, what we are doing when we consider bills like Bill C-122 that is establishing industrial policy, as much as the government opposite would suggest we are not doing anything.
The free trade agreement, the NAFTA and others are expressions of industrial policy. This plant was identified as one of the most efficient in North America and certainly the most efficient in Canada. It was the most productive, the most cost efficient. All of the accolades and adjectives that go with an economic and financial environment were applied to this plant.
Someone made a decision who was outside the boundaries of our country, outside the range of our political system and outside the patriotic emotions that keep people here and make them responsible corporate and private citizens. Someone outside those parameters suggested and effected a guillotine on 3,500 jobs.
There were 3,500 families no longer with incomes. Close to $50 million in tax revenues were lost. A similar amount per annum at least over the course of the next year in social benefits must be paid out at a cost to the taxpayer. I ask my colleague: What should we encourage the government opposite to do when faced with such faulty industrial policy?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence for the question.
I have enjoyed the last five years being a member of Parliament. It has been a great experience and I thank my community for the privilege. However I will say one thing has really bothered me about my experience being an MP. It is that I believe the lobby system is out of control. For the people who are watching, lobbyists are usually paid a large amount of money to work on bureaucrats, MPs and ministers to make sure their particular objective is met. The lobbyists who tend to be the most successful are the ones who get the most money. They have the best access and usually as a result have the most impact on government.
Let us face it that the people who have the most money are the larger corporations and they tend to be transnationals. These transnational companies are basically circumventing the elected members of Parliament.
I have to say that I know members of Parliament in the Conservative Party who share my view about lobbyists. We need to review the Lobbyists Registration Act and we need an accountable and transparent system so that we know what is going on.
Only when we get that part of the economy organized can we get to deal with the real reasons decisions were taken like the one on the Scarborough van plant.

Mr. Speaker, what are we doing here this morning? My constituents might ask that question. I want to give them an idea of precisely what occurs in the House on occasion and what we as their representatives are asked to do.
Today we are talking about Bill C-122, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, textile tariff reduction. If that is not the title of a bill that whets one's appetite for further investigation then nothing is. I am sure everybody in Scarborough West is sitting on the edge of their seats to find out what in Heaven's name is in the bill.
I say that sarcastically. I point out to my constituents and to those listening that there are 327 pages in this legislation and it is just an amendment to the Customs Fhriff. Of those 327 pages only the first 8 deal with specific amendments to specific sections. Of those first 8 pages, 5 are simply a series of numbers which would look as if they have been generated by a computer in some game or in some child's mind.
What does that mean? It means this bill was brought forward for first reading on April 19, 1993. That is less than a month ago. Here we are considering it for second reading debate, which is approval in principle, in May. Why? One might ask why. How do we as members of Parliament, as political parties and as critics decide whether or not to approve a bill like this one in principle? That is what I want to discuss this afternoon. It is how we come to these decisions.
We often hear those who are critics of this place and of the parliamentary system saying that we should reflect the views of our constituents. I do not disagree, but are
May 11, 1993

we mere voting machines of the parties as some would allege or are we mere voting machines of the majority of the electorate as others would like us to be?
If we are the latter and are simply sent here to reflect what the majority at any given time wants us to say without in any way thinking about the issues ourselves then I ask the people of Canada: What should we do with Bill C-122? I ask the people of Canada to tell us what to do with 327 pages of amendments, 99 per cent of which are numbers and relate to previous tariffs. What do the people of Canada want us to do? Do we hold a referendum and find out what the people of Canada want us to do on Bill C-122? How do the people of Canada come to a decision as to whether or not we should support in principle Bill C-122?
I think I made my point. The people of Scarborough West and all other people of Canada sent members of Parliament here not only to reflect the will of the majority at any particular time. They gave us the responsibility to investigate a bill such as Bill C-122 and in fact all bills. They gave us the responsibility to sit on committees to examine all 327 pages of this bill and the existing Customs Tariff upon which this act is based and to come to a reasoned decision on whether or not the bill in principle should be allowed to proceed through the House of Commons. That is what they sent us here to do. At least that is my proposition.
If we assume for a moment that is accurate, how do I as the member of Parliament for Scarborough West approach an examination of Bill C-122 on whether or not we should have approval in principle? Obviously we have to know what it is all about, and we know it is about the Customs Thriff.
Many people will know that one cannot be an expert on everything in this world. In fact there are very few people who are experts on anything in this world. Where do we go? What do we do? I must confess that one of my burning interests is not the amendments to the Customs Tariff.
All parties have people who are responsible for different areas of legislation. We look to them to give us some advice and guidance as to what we should be looking at. In this case the Official Opposition critic for revenue under which this bill falls is my colleague from Eglin-ton-Lawrence. He has been charged with the responsibility by the Liberal Party of reviewing this legislation and making certain recommendations to us as to what we
Government Orders
should be doing. Indeed he has done that and he has done a very fine job. However we are independent people. We have the opportunity to review a piece of legislation like this one and come to our own independent conclusions. Our critic has provided us with the opportunity to do so because he has given us background information on this material.
I want to go through this so that the people of Scarborough West and those who are listening can see how we analyse a bill like this one and the listeners can come to their conclusions as they may.
What is the background of Bill C-122? The Minister of Finance at some point in the history of the world decided that he would direct the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. Everything has a short form. In this case the Canadian International Trade Tribunal is CUT He directed it to provide him with advice on how to reduce textile tariffs down to levels comparable with those of Canada's major industrialized trading partners. We will leave the issue of why he directed them to do that for a moment.
What did CITT find out? CITT found out that the average most favoured nation textile tariff for Canada was 15.7 per cent compared to 10.5 per cent for the U.S. One might ask: "So what? What does that mean?" One has to put it in context.
Of course these are the people who have some interest in this textile industry. They have some knowledge in the textile industry. They make their living at it so one would hope when they did their investigations they would come up with some reasoned recommendations, and indeed they did.
First, they recommended that Canadian textile tariffs be reduced by an average of 26 per cent by moving to a simpler rate structure with maximum duties of 5 per cent for fibres, 10 per cent for yams and 16 per cent for fabrics. I confess I do not know too much about fibres, yams and fabrics. I rely on Cm to make that recommendation.
Second, they recommended that the average tariff on speciality textiles be reduced by 33 per cent and that a complex annually calculated rate on certain wool fabrics be fixed at 11.8 per cent. So what? What would happen? Under these proposals average Canadian textile tariffs would remain higher than U.S. duties and be significant-

ly higher than those of Japan or the European Economic Community.
Nothing much happened but they made a third recommendation. This may be why nothing much happened for the time being. CITE agreed with the Canadian Textiles Institute-another group of people who are interested in this particular subject matter-that the implementation of the tariff cuts they recommended should wait until the current round of GATT negotiations had been completed.
What is the GATT? There is another series of initials. It means the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. It is a large international body that discusses tariff and trade issues. In any event they recommended that until those GATT negotiations had been completed the tariff cuts should wait. Why? It was in order to make full use of the proposed tariff reductions as bargaining levers in the negotiations.
Are we waiting? No, we are not. Here we are talking about Bill C-122 today, in May 1993. It is one month before a leadership convention will choose a new Prime Minister and certainly not more than two or three months from the next general election. Where is the fire? What is the hurry? Why do we have to deal with this bill today? Why is the House not dealing with something else today? Hopefully we can find out by looking at the bill.
What does the bill do? I have reduced these 327 pages down to a manageable few pages simply so that I can handle it. To absorb this in one sitting is asking too much.
Here is the first thing it does. It would phase in the tariff reductions that CITT recommended at the rate of 1.5 percentage points per year rather than the 1 percentage point recommended by CITT. Why and when? There is no explanation for why it is half a percentage point higher. It would start January 1, 1993 and not January 1, 1994. It is retroactive legislation, which is something that is anathema to the House most times. This is unless we are talking for example about Bill C-91 because in that case it is perfectly okay to back date legislation as far as drug patents are concerned. Here we have back dating again, January 1, 1993.
The second thing the bill would do is treat specialty textiles and certain lightweight wool fabrics in the same manner as other fibres, yarns and fabrics. What manner
might that be? 'tariffs would be reduced to maximum rates of 5 per cent, 10 per cent and 16 per cent respectively.
Finally the legislation would maintain the margins of tariff preference for trade with Australia and New Zealand on six tariff items in which there is significant trade.
What am I supposed to do? How am I supposed to decide on behalf of the constituents of Scarborough West whether what I have just said is an excellent idea, whether this House should approve it in principle and whether I should vote to approve it in principle? How do we put it into context?
Let us look at the section. Forget the sections that have innumerable numbers. Let us read this interesting section which is section 4. If Bill C-115 introduced in the third session of the 34th Parliament and entitled "an act to implement the North American Free Trade Agreement" is assented to, schedule I to the Customs Thriff as enacted by that act is amended.
One whole section deals with various amendments to the Customs Tariff if the NAFTA is assented to. I ask again: Where is the fire? What is the hurry? I know what the hurry is. We are in the dying days of a Parliament with a dying government. It wants to-and I use the words advisedly-ram through with the least amount of debate the NAFTA and all peripheral legislation that supports it.
We know the NAFTA is not supposed to come into force until January 1, 1994. That is in the future. At least we are dealing with a piece of legislation that is going to be in the future, we hope. This bill wants to go back a year earlier to January 1, 1993. It mandates certain actions if the NAFTA is passed.
What if the NAFTA is passed by this Parliament but is not acceded to by the United States? Do we have to come back and amend this? It says: "If Bill C-115, introduced in the third session of the 34th Parliament and entitled NAFTA is assented to, schedule I to the Customs Tariff as enacted by that act is amended". What do we do? Do we pass the act and let it sit on the shelf until it is assented to, presumably after the United States has agreed to it?
May 11, 1993

If we are going to have it sit on the shelf anyway and wait for royal assent, why do we not give the people of Canada an opportunity to decide whether they wish to proceed with the NAFTA and have royal assent to some piece of legislation that is building on a foundation that may never be there? What is the point of discussing this bill, taking up the time of the House when we are really talking about legislation that implements certain aspects of the North American free trade agreement?
I ask my constituents what they would have me do when we are voting on principle of the legislation.
Resign.
The hon. Solicitor General says: "Resign". That will not be up to the hon. Solicitor General but to the good people of Scarborough West.
He is echoing what his constituents are telling him.

At least the hon. Solicitor General is finally listening to what the Official Opposition critic of the Solicitor General has to say. I congratulate him for that.
How do I determine whether or not we should approve this bill in principle? I guess we have to see what it is going to do and what various industries that will be most affected are going to do. What is their point of view?
We are told the textile industry took the view that if the tariff reductions were to proceed they should be delayed as long as possible and back end loaded-I guess that is an industry term-with the weight of duty reductions imposed in the second half of the 1990s. It is now 1993, which is not in the second half of the 1990s.
The view of the textile industry would permit more time to adjust to the free trade agreement reductions. Any proposed tariff cuts under the GATT negotiations should also become evident by that time, including any relaxation of the multi-fibre arrangement.
What about Canadian clothing manufacturers who also have an interest in this bill? They would have preferred to see larger tariff cuts implemented immediately, although they were prepared to accept a five-year phase in period.
