We have a little bit of controversy within the industry as to which way we should be going. The Canadian textile institute, which has some interest in these topics, believes the unilateral tariff cuts at this time are "inappropriate and potentially damaging" to the Canadian textile industry. There is something we can hang our hats on.
To a person who does not know too much about this industry like me and is being asked on behalf of my constituents to decide whether we should approve this in principle, that carries a significant amount of weight because it is the people in the industry who are making these comments.
What sort of ramifications would occur? The bill fails to address the need for deep tariff cuts on fabrics which are not available in Canada. For example, the most favoured nation duty on imports of most broad weave cotton fabrics will be cut from 17.5 per cent to 16 per cent. Yet according to a particular expert in the industry these fabrics are no longer manufactured in Canada. What does that mean? Does that mean it is not a relevant provision?
It means that when we have difficult pieces of legislation like this one we do not want them brought forward in the dying days of a Parliament based on an agreement which is yet to become law, presupposing it is going to become law, only to have it sit on the shelf until it is given royal assent.
Under all of these circumstances it has become clear to the person best informed in my party, namely the Official Opposition critic for revenue, the hon. member from Eglinton-Lawrence, that we should not approve this bill in principle for some of the reasons I have enumerated. That is how the process works as far as I am concerned in terms of determining whether or not I should accept a bill in principle.
From my perspective based on the advice given to me and the analysis I have done, I will not be supporting this bill in principle.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's remarks certainly reflect my own thinking in this case. Anything that comes before this House that will deepen and widen the effects of the free trade deal already in place or serve to entrench what is going to happen under the NAFTA legislation is something that my party and I are 100 per cent opposed to.

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
We are opposed for a number of reasons. Certainly what has happened to the manufacturing industry including the textile industry is one of them. The facts and figures are clear. Since the FTA came in we have lost 23 per cent of our manufacturing jobs, including massive job losses in the textile industry.
Although the government may argue these losses are due to world-wide recession, that argument is revealed as bogus by the fact in the same period of time the United States has only lost 6 per cent of its manufacturing capacity. The loss of manufacturing jobs since the FTA came in almost ranks with the job loss that occurred during the Great Depression of the 1930s when 29 per cent of the manufacturing jobs were lost.
Some people may ask how this loss of manufacturing capacity affects a constituency like my own in northern Saskatchewan, Prince Albert-Churchill River. Certainly we do not have a great deal of textile manufacturing in the constituency. We do have one small plant which is an Indian owned organization called Silver Mountain Industries. It is doing very well because perhaps Indian people are more sensible than the rest of Canadians and tend to support their own, which Canadians in general could do well to learn. Nevertheless free trade which has caused the loss of manufacturing capacity has hurt my constituency by what it has done to the economic structure of the country.
The economy of the prairie provinces, particularly Saskatchewan, has always been very dependent on resources. Therefore the economy is subject to a great number of fluctuations because resource prices and commodity prices tend to rise and fall dramatically.
The whole process of equalization has always been the strength of this country and has always maintained the ability of the people of Saskatchewan to enjoy the same standard of living as the rest of Canadians. The process of equalization has always depended on manufacturing in Ontario doing well through good times and bad times. It has always been the stabilizing point of Canadian economic life.
I would like to challenge the member as a member of the Liberal caucus. Elis caucus has taken the position that the free trade deal and legislation like this that flows from it should be renegotiated. Flow does the hon. member's party propose to renegotiate the free trade agreement when the Americans have no incentive to renegotiate? They have already won everything they
wanted, particularly the control of our resources under the existing free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting how my hon. friend the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River has managed to ask a question on Liberal philosophy when we are talking about Bill C-122, dealing with amendments to the Customs Tariff.
Far be it for me to ever shirk from a legitimate question, so let me answer the question. It is very simple. In any series of negotiations one simply approaches the other side and asks if they will open up negotiations because of certain sore points that have developed which could not have been foreseen, were not foreseen or discussed at the time the original agreement was entered into.	,
Of course we can talk about the future, I put to the hon. member very frankly. One sits down with the American trade representatives and says: "Look, it has been five years. We do not have a definition of subsidy. We do not know what we are talking about with antidumping. Every time the Canadians seem to do something good, your industry gets into a tizzy and takes us right to the final arbiter before you back down and pay back the tariffs that you have illegally taken from us".
If the Americans were to say, perchance: "Drop dead, we have you by the throat", we always have the option that the hon. member's party has as its only option, to get rid of the deal and abrogate. We do not need to get to that point because that automatically assumes bad faith on the part of our greatest trading partner. There is no reason to assume bad faith. In fact we should assume good faith until bad faith is proven.
We simply sit down with our counterparts in the United States, point out the sore points and ask them if they will renegotiate. Should they take a bull-headed, hard-headed unreasonable, unexplainable position, we still have the opportunity to abrogate.
I say that is the Liberal position, unlike the fawning position of the Tories which is to simply lie down and sign the deal without in any way dealing with the very major problems in the FTA on which it is based. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the late Harold Danforth.
Mr. Danforth served fellow Canadians as a member of Parliament for the riding of Kent and the riding of Essex-Kent for 15 years between 1958 and 1974. Prior to his service in the House of Commons, Mr. Danforth had a successful career both as a farmer and a municipal councillor.
His keen interest in agriculture was an integral part of Mr. Danforth's life and this was evident in many of his accomplishments. Educated at the Ontario Agricultural College, he was able to combine his formal and practical farming experience not only in the operation of his own farm but also as a member of the Institute of Professional Agrologists, President of the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Growers' Association, Chairman of the Blenheim District Agriculture Fair, Director of the Kent-Elgin New Potato Marketing Board, Chairman of the Seacliff Growers Co-op, South Essex Growers' Co-op and the Essex County Federation of Agriculture.
Mr. Danforth's distinguished parliamentary career included his service as the Conservative critic for agriculture and chairman of the agriculture committee and committee of trade and commerce.
Throughout his public life, Mr. Danforth's emphasis was on serving the needs of his constituency. His diligence and thoughtful approach to public service set an example for his peers. He shall be remembered for his contributions and respected for his accomplishments.
It is with sadness that we mourn the loss of our colleague, Harold Danforth. But his memory shall live in the hearts of his family and friends, and his contributions to this institution and the betterment of Canadians shall live on forever.

I had the privilege of serving with him from 1965 until the 1974 general election. From the time we first met it was apparent that we had a lot of things in common. He had a farm background and had served in various positions on the fair boards and local and provincial federations of agriculture. He was veiy committed to the agricultural community and had served on municipal council before entering politics.
I remember Harold as a kind man who placed an emphasis on duty to his constituents. He had a way about him that made him very approachable and his jovial nature attracted people to him.

Harold Danforth certainly made the best of his life. He made the world a better place in which to live for those whom he touched.
On behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party, I express my condolences to his family and friends. Harold may be gone but his memories will remain in these halls forever.

Mr. Speaker, just a word on behalf of the New Democratic Party. I remember Harold Danforth veiy well. When I was first elected in 1968 he had been a member of Parliament since 1958. He sat over here as the Conservative Party's agriculture critic.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of reflection upon reading Bill C-122 that I rise to speak today. The purpose of this bill which is called an act to amend the customs tariff precisely with the textile tariff reduction, is supposed to bring Canadian textile tariffs more into line with textile tariffs in other industrialized economies.
These reductions are supposed to benefit the Canadian economy by making Canada's apparel and other textile-using industries more competitive. The tariff changes we will be discussing this afternoon are also supposed to benefit consumers by lowering the cost of clothing and other finished products.
I said "supposed to" in prefacing my remarks in the last two examples. I want to explain why I am saying that. I do not believe that these tariff reductions will make clothing less expensive. I do not believe it will make Canadian workers more competitive. I do believe that if we pass this customs tariff act, Bill C-122, we will be putting many more workers in the textile industry out of work.
I would like to stress the point that the NDP is not against freer trade. We are in favour of fair trade. If you look at the bill before us, you are looking at the clearest example of unfair trade as has been brought before this House in many a year.
It boggles the mind that when we have so much unemployment we are presenting a bill to lower tariffs.

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
This will affect the textile industry which has been devastated to such a degree in my province that the government has not even been able to come up with a sufficient amount of money to provide a cushion for those workers who are supposed to have been recycled under government programs. That was the promise the government gave us initially when it proceeded with the free trade agreement.
Further on in this tariff reduction act that we are asked to support by the government we will also have NAFTA coming in-I will explain how it comes in-which further complicates the possibility of our textile industry surviving.
Canadian textile tariffs are not, as the government's 1988 policy decision assumed, twice as high as the textile tariffs of other industrialized countries, including our major trading partner the United States. That is what this bill is all about, unilateral tariff reductions taken by Canada. For the first time we see both labour and industry united in opposing a particular bill. They are opposed to it because they do not think that reducing these textile tariffs is appropriate at this time. They see it as potentially damaging to our industry.
The tariff negotiations we have already had normally would put us in a good position to get something in return for our tariff reductions. Remember that Bill C-122 is a tariff reduction bill. What are we getting? We are getting absolutely nothing from our other trading partners. In fact, even calling this a kind of trade negotiation is a misnomer because there is hardly any negotiation.
We are saying to the United States, and under NAFTA we are saying to Mexico, that Canada is open for business; come and get it. We want you to compete. We are lowering our tariffs. Come in, even if it means the ruination of our textile industry in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada. So be it.
That is what the government calls free trade. I call it unfair trade. I believe that if this bill is passed it is going to be the final nail in the coffin of the textile industry in Quebec, which I speak for, and elsewhere across the country. It is a very unfair bill.
The Minister for International Trade said during the Uruguay round transition that the government will ensure the textile and clothing industries, and I quote
the minister, "will enjoy over-all protection equivalent to what is available to our major trading partners, particularly the United States".
This is not so. The textile industry in this country will be put at a tremendous disadvantage with this unilateral reduction of tariffs in the textile industry. We will be inundated by Mexican clothing imports. The factories we already have are smaller factories rather than larger factories. Most of the factories have less than 20 workers and many have four or five workers. The industry is going to continue to be fragmented and it is going to be very difficult for workers to survive in this industry.
Let me give a little bit of a history about how this bill came about. Bill C-122 is an act to amend the Customs Tariff (textile tariff reduction). It was introduced in the House of Commons on April 19, 1993, less than one month ago. It has been speedily put through the House mainly because the government sees it as a major response to the United States and other countries coming into the free trade agreement and with Mexico coming into the NAFTA.
This bill comes as a result of the tariff reduction recommendations that were made to the Minister of Finance by the Canadian International Trade Tribunal back in February 1990. So we are dealing with this a little bit more than three years after the initial free trade agreement. There is no doubt about it that this is, if not the son of free trade, one of the cousins or daughters of free trade because we are going to see more and more of these bills. They are a kind of quid pro quo agreements with the United States as we get these so-called advantages, although I am not quite sure we have really received that many advantages from the free trade agreement.
When the Senate conducted a study of the free trade agreement it looked at the advantages and disadvantages and was not able to come up with any advantages or disadvantages because it found the picture too cloudy. Once we see the other trade-offs we will be engaging in, and this Bill C-122 is one of those trade-offs, we are going to be more easily able to see what the trade-offs are as far as jobs are concerned. We are going to be trading jobs all the way down into Mexico. They are going to go there and to the United States.

If we had a finance minister who really protected Canadian workers' interests first we could have had not a free trade but a fair trade agreement with the United States, Mexico and other countries under which we would protect our workers, particularly our textile workers. No, this government is not interested in fair trade.
In analysing the bill in a technical sense I would like to give the following highlights. Bill C-122 would implement the Canadian International Trade Tribunal recommendations with some modifications. First, starting on January 1, 1993 legislation would phase in the tariff reductions at the rate of 1.5 percentage points a year. That has been stalled a bit because we are getting into the bill a little bit later now. However the important thing to remember is that the Canadian International Trade Tribunal recommended that we only lower the percentage by one percentage point a year for a maximum of six years. We are actually reducing tariff rates on textiles by a much higher percentage than even the CUT, the Canadian International Trade Tribunal, suggested.
We are in such an all-fired hurry to get this tariff reduction bill passed in order to get on friendlier terms with the United States that we are even willing to exceed recommendations that I would assume were prudent and reasonable by about 50 per cent.
Second, Bill C-122 would treat specialty textiles and certain lightweight wool fabrics in the same manner as other fabrics, fibres and yarns. The tariffs would be reduced to maximum rates of 5 per cent, 10 per cent and 16 per cent respectively. The tariffs are currently at 8,13 and 18 to 25 per cent respectively.
It would seem at first glance that the tariff reductions are not all that great, but when it gets down to the average piece of clothing then we are looking at substantial reductions and at the same time we are looking at substantial losses leading to a loss of jobs.
I previously said that industry and labour were united in their opposition. I should have been more precise. I am talking primarily about the major unions in Quebec and Ontario but I am also talking about the CTI, the
Government Orders
Canadian Textile Institute, which is the primary challenger of this legislation.
The Canadian Textile Institute is one of the major industry associations. It does not encompass all of the firms but is one of the major industry associations that has challenged the need for any tariff reductions. The Canadian Textile Institute does not think that tariff reductions are necessary. It understands because it is in the industry. It understands just how severely devastated the textile industry is across Canada.
Here for the first time we see a rather strange comradeship between business people and unions opposed to a bill that would lower tariffs on textiles. I say it is strange because we do not see it that often, but we do not see legislation that is so devastating that often and Bill C-122 would have that effect.
I can understand why the Canadian Textile Institute would challenge the need for any tariff reductions. It is having enough problems with unemployment and competition as things stand right now.
When the fait accompli was placed before the Canadian Textile Institute, and I am talking about Bill C-122, it took the view that if tariff reductions were to proceed anyhow then these reductions should be delayed as long as possible and back end loaded with the weight of duty reductions imposed in the second half of the 1990s.
It is being fairly conservative here because it does not want this thing to hit it all at once. It is not prepared for it. I do not believe the government has any programs to provide the cushion these workers are going to need, that fantastic cushion we were promised three years ago that would help workers who need to be recycled and would help workers who need to get into industries to have the training to get into other industries in which they would have more of a future. We have not seen those programs.
I believe the Canadian Textile Institute when it is saying that if we are going to reduce tariffs let us do it in a slower way than is proposed in this bill. It was reflecting its concern about how little is out there for those workers who are going to be displaced. Many of those workers in the textile industry are women who are going to be thrown out of their jobs and are going to have to look for some recycling into other jobs and the government is not

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
there for them. The Canadian Textile Institute is well aware of this potential problem.
The Canadian Textile Institute also has manifested a great deal of concern over the free trade agreement generally and the harm it has initially done to the textile industry. It is concerned that this addition to the free trade agreement would cause the industry even greater harm.
The Canadian Textile Institute does propose that any proposed tariff cuts under the GATT negotiation should also become evident by that time, which is later, including any relaxation of the multi-fibre arrangement.
It is essentially saying let us slow down, let us take a look at these tariff reductions in a general way, let us perhaps go with what the Canadian International Trade Tribunal said, which is that the percentages be less than they are and not 1.5 percentage points but 1 percentage point. By gaining time, we would see under the GATT negotiations whether there would be any relaxation of the agreements that we have under the multi-fibre arrangement.
The Canadian International Trade Tribunal appeared initially in its recommendations to favour a compromise between the positions of the clothing makers and the textile industry. I should say that the clothing makers and the textile industry are a bit opposed on Bill C-122. The apparel manufacturers are in favour of it. The textile manufacturers are against it and they are the ones who are linking arms with the unions in order to preserve jobs in the textile industry.
The Canadian International Trade Tribunal in giving its reasons for a slower approach was well aware of the fact that by any quick reduction of tariffs we could dislocate this industry to an extent that recovery would be next to impossible.
The Canadian Textile Institute in defending its position as to why it is opposed to this bill gives four reasons.
I think the four reasons bear looking into today when we are looking at this bill.
First, the Canadian Textile Institute says that general preferential rates of duty, called the GPT, for textile imports from less developed countries does not apply the generalized system of preferences to textile imports.
Second, Canada provides lower duty rates for certain textile imports under schedule 2 of the Customs Tariff already.
Third, Canada has duty remission programs affecting import of fabrics used in garment manufacturing while the U.S. does not have any such programs.
Fourth, the free trade agreement tariff reductions have had a greater impact on Canadian trade-weighted tariffs because more than half of Canadian textile imports are purchased from the U.S. while just 8 per cent of U.S. textile imports are from Canada.
Finally, as if that was not enough to demonstrate the disadvantages that Canada is already suffering in the textile industry vis-a-vis the United States, the United States has a more extensive quota system on textiles than Canada. This type of import protection is not captured when simply comparing tariff rates.
It is obvious we need to compete in a global economy. It is obvious we need to have fairer trade before free trade. We need to lower tariffs but at the same time, and this is the one thing that has escaped this government, we need to look out for the people who are going to be most displaced, dislocated, and thrown out, and many times at an age, 40 or 50 years old, when it is very difficult to recycle.
The face of poverty and the face of unemployment is no longer the odd person who does not want to work. The faces of unemployment today are our brothers, sisters, families, and neighbours. We see it every day. When it comes time to making this country of ours more competitive we have to keep in mind that there is a fragile balance between free trade and unemployment and keeping people with jobs. This government has lost track of that subtle, fragile balance and that is the reason we have over one million unemployed people.
I would suggest that this bill go to committee. Perhaps there is something we can salvage from it. This kind of unilateral tariff reduction when we do not get anything in exchange, which will do so much to harm textile workers, has been a hallmark of this government's approach to the economy. It seems not to be concerned about the walking wounded of its policies but with currying favour in other countries.
I am against this particular bill but I will allow it to go to committee.

May 11, 1993

Mr. Speaker, for many years the textile industry in Montreal has been profoundly important to the growth and development of our city. It has been a driving force in an economic engine that has stalled under the economic mismanagement of the Conservative government.
Under nine years of Tory rule the textile industry in Montreal has suffered immeasurably. Thousands of men and women have been thrown out of work because of the failure of the Conservatives to address the real problems facing the Canadian textile industry.
Bill C-122 was introduced subsequent to the disastrous economic statement tabled by the Minister of Finance last December. The purpose of this bill is to implement the changes proposed by the Canadian International Trade Tribunal.
We have to ask ourselves why we are moving ahead with the reduction of tariffs at this particular time. We are hurting our own textile industry on the assumption that the North American free trade agreement will be a fact of life. Well, it is not a signed deal and I do not know why the Conservatives are assuming that it is.
The contempt that they have shown for this Parliament is remarkable. They have included provisions in this bill that will not come into effect until after certain agreements have been made both as a result of the GATT and the North American free trade agreement. Why are we giving up this potential bargaining chip so easily?
One really has to wonder how or why this government has managed to conduct the negotiations in the interests of Canadians if it is willing to sign on the dotted line before agreements have been reached on either NAFTA or on the GATT.
The government tries to tell us that this bill will protect Canadian firms' competitive advantage. No one could be opposed to that especially if that were in fact the case. However as with many other things that this government does it only tells us half the story. It does not tell us that this bill is taking away from one industry in favour of another. We know that it does not have to proceed with these tariff reductions until it is obliged to either by the GATT or any other trade agreement.
Government Orders
If we are trying to address the cost inputs for the clothing manufacturing industry that is only one side of the story. We also have to look at how this will affect the textile producing industry in this country.
If we unilaterally reduce the tariffs to the benefit of one industry at the expense of another all we are doing is robbing Peter to pay Paul. Hardly a just thing to do.
What are we doing? Are we lowering the tariffs to appease our neighbours to the south once again? It seems that as soon as there is a request from the United States for Canada to provide American manufacturers with an advantage, the Conservatives are only too happy to oblige.
The people of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville simply do not trust this government to negotiate on behalf of Canadians because they know Conservatives are willing to sell all of us short.
They are willing to sacrifice the protection of our industry without any benefit for Canadians. This is typical of how the Conservatives have dreadfully mismanaged our economy. It is this total regard for the common Canadian worker that has devastated the Canadian economy and has created a sense of mistrust for politicians.
It is time for this government to stand up to the lobbyists and work in the interests of all Canadians. Even the CITT suggested that we wait until the passage of the North American free trade agreement and the anticipated changes to the GATT, before we go ahead with these amendments to the tariffs on textiles coming into this country from overseas, and more importantly textiles imported from the United States and Mexico. We must move more slowly and deliberately in the treatment of this issue. Thousands of jobs in Quebec depend on how we proceed today. We must put this whole issue on hold. We have to wait to see how the United States Congress deals with the North American free trade agreement before we commit ourselves directly to these proposed changes.
What is the rush? We are here to represent the interests of Canadians and quite frankly I do not see any advantage here for the people of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville, nor for anyone else in Quebec.

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
Since this government came to power the direction of Canadian trade policy has worked against the interests of all Canadians. Conservative trade policy has resulted in record high unemployment, millions of Canadians on social assistance and a sense of despair that has to be turned around.
Canada should be an open and active trading nation. We should not, however, be irresponsible in our trading practices. We must not lay all of our cards on the table to the advantage of our competitors. We must do whatever we can to give Canadians and Canadian industry an advantage in a global economy.
The textile industry has argued that if tariff reductions were to proceed they should be delayed as long as possible and back end loaded with the weight of duty reductions imposed. This would give them time to adjust to the new rules and be fair to them and their employees.
The Canadian Textile Institute does not oppose the reduction of tariffs. They believe that the government should take a more intelligent and careful course of action. They do believe that unilateral cuts are "inappropriate and potentially damaging to the Canadian textile industry".
I share this industry's concern. I do not understand why the government is proceeding with tariff reductions at this time when it knows full well that the result of their actions could be more unemployment, more hardship and less opportunity for Canadians.
We have to go back to the drawing board. We have to start from scratch. It has to go to the negotiating table with our trading partners for the North American free trade agreement and the GATT with the attitude that Canadian jobs and Canadian workers come first.
If the Conservatives do not want to take on that challenge it is time that they step aside and give the opportunity to a government that cares for average Canadian workers and their families. It should give a chance to a government that knows how hard it is to hold a job in an increasingly competitive global economy.
I say no to this bill because it will hurt the people of my riding and my province. I say no to this bill because it is ill-conceived and brought forward at the wrong time. Let us hope the committee can do something to change it.
Canadians come first, at least in my book. It is time that the Conservatives learned the same thing. To do any
less would be a betrayal of Canadian workers and companies and I want no part of it.

Mr. Speaker, it is pretty clear the Tory government is at the end of its term and is going all out to please everybody, especially the Americans, while neglecting Canadian industry. If clothing manufacturers will benefit somewhat, textile manufacturers will lose on this deal.
What happens when we have to manufacture Canadian clothing without being able to find fabric made in Canada? Is this how the Canadian economy is supposed to recover? Is this how the country will become economically strong? I doubt it.
Once again, we have a bill that strikes at Quebec and especially at the greater Montreal area, where unemployment is bad enough as it is.
This government is proving, day in day out, that it has no idea of what running a country involves. Canadians are fed up, and in the next election, they will vote in a new government that will make this country economically stable.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-89 proposes three amendments to the Investment Canada Act which reflect the increasing role and importance of investment to Canada's prosperity.
These amendments are intended to help Canadian companies attract the capital and technology they need to grow and compete while protecting our sensitive cultural sector. The first amendment will extend to investors in the oil and gas sectors the same review thresholds that apply to other sectors of the Canadian economy under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
For U.S. investors this will raise the thresholds above which a direct acquisition becomes subject to the act. There is no review for indirect acquisitions. All other international investors' thresholds for review will remain unchanged. The over-all result will be an enhancement of the value of the resource base for all investors and a stronger Canadian exploration and producing industry.
The second proposed amendment will enable Investment Canada to enter into agreements with Canadian companies or business associations to share the costs of programs and initiatives designed to attract international capital and technologies to those same Canadian companies.
Such international investments and investment partners are critical to the ability of Canadian companies to compete, grow and provide jobs for Canadians. Investment Canada facilitates deals between Canadian companies and the international investors as part of the federal government's investment development program.
An increasing number of Canadian companies and business associations is now prepared to share the costs of seeking international investment and funding investment partners.
The third amendment relates that the support of a strong cultural sector is a priority of this government. The amendment will give the minister new powers to determine whether or not a business entity in the cultural sector is Canadian controlled.
Government Orders
The retroactive provisions are designed to discourage an investor from quickly completing an investment which could not withstand the scrutiny of the minister using new powers as of June 19, 1992.
To summarize, the main thrust of these amendments to the Investment Canada Act is to increase the attractiveness of Canada's investment environment and facilitate the cost-sharing between the private sector and governments in seeking investment initiatives. Thus Canada will continue to grow as an attractive investment destination and I commend this legislation to all members.

Mr. Speaker, this bill cleans up a few small problems that have come to light under the regime of Investment Canada. As such, it is difficult to take exception to what it has done specifically here.
This government has failed to come to grips with the real economic issues of Canada. Part of its economic approach to creating jobs and growth in Canada since it took office in 1984 was to get rid of Investment Canada which screened foreign takeovers of our already very heavily foreign-owned Canadian economy. It was to screen them to insist that there be a significant benefit for Canada if there was going to be another takeover. It replaced the Foreign Investment Review Agency with Investment Canada. The government says it was designed to encourage more investment and particularly more takeovers of Canadian industries.
The result we have seen is that since June 30, 1985 when Investment Canada replaced FIRA, we have seen a total of over 6,000 takeovers and new businesses started. But the new businesses started by foreign owners have only been 30 per cent of the total.
When there is an international takeover by foreigners with a foreign head office, Canadian industry becomes extremely vulnerable. Having practised tax law in this area for a number of years, I know the tricks that are used. I am quite familiar with most of the ways revenue can be bled out of Canada to get it free of Canadian tax into either offshore jurisdictions or the home country.
We have also found in this period of downturn in the global economy that, when rationalization takes place it is the Canadian branch plants that get rationalized out of

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
existence. Over the past four years we have seen the deindustrialization of Canada with the loss of 16 per cent of our manufacturing jobs and those are the best jobs we have.
The Tories try to blame world economic conditions, globalization or whatever. We can say these are factors over which Canadians have no control and therefore they are just going to take place anyway. But during the same period that we have lost 15 per cent of our manufacturing jobs, how do the Tories explain that the Americans have lost only 6 per cent of their manufacturing jobs? Our jobs have gone south.
It is important that we try to indicate why this has happened. What lessons can we learn from nine years of Tory government and why have we lost so many jobs? Why is the economic future of Canada dim, especially for the thousands upon thousands of Canadians who were active members of the work force and can no longer get a job? Thousands upon thousands of young Canadians are graduating from our post-secondary schools, CEGEPs, high schools or universities and have no hope of getting a job here in Canada.
Since 1989 Canada's ability to compete globally has fallen from 4th to 11th place. Since 1984 when the Tories took office our manufacturing productivity has grown at only two-thirds the rate of the manufacturing productivity in the G-7 countries that are our biggest competitors.
In that nine-year period we have seen our high-tech trade, which is really an indication of our future ability to compete, go from a surplus of $1 billion in 1984 to a deficit of $30 billion last year.
The Tories make much of the fact that they have the fundamentals right and our trade is picking up. When they took office in 1984 our trade surplus was $19.8 billion. Last year it was $7.4 billion.
This government has emphasized the umbrella or macro policies and what has happened? Its obsession with the deficit, which has failed to produce a reduced deficit. Its deficit to this day is about what it was when it took office. Meanwhile, Canada's federal public debt has grown from about $170 billion to $470 billion.
Its monetary policy has emphasized driving every ounce of inflation out of our economy. It has jacked up interest rates to their highest spread over U.S. rates that Canada has ever seen. At many times over the past four
years Canadian interest rates in real terms, taking inflation into account, were more than 6 percentage points higher than the American rates.
What has been the effect of this? First of all Canadians were at a real competitive disadvantage vis-a-vis their major competitors, the Americans, when it came to borrowing to upgrade their plants and equipment and expand. So our manufacturers were hamstrung.
In terms of the public debt, a recent study has shown that if the Tories during their terms in office had kept Canada's interest rates at the historic spread of about two percentage points higher than American rates, their deficit next year, instead of being $34 billion as predicted by the Minister of Finance, would be $4 billion. That is because the added cost of interest on the debt is one of the biggest nuts that has to be broken. Their monetary policy has not worked.
With regard to their fiscal policy, there have been over 35 tax increases since the Tories took power, the last one being the GST.
The Liberals do not claim to have supported the previous tax, the federal sales tax or the manufacturers' sales tax as it was called. In certain cases-and we admit to this-it penalized domestic production over importation. There were ways the Tories could have dealt with that and gotten rid of it, but instead they went for wholesale tax reform and gave us the goods and services tax.
They could not have brought in a worse tax at a worse time in Canada's history. First of all this tax required the government to hire an extra 4,000 federal public servants to introduce, implement and administer the GST. It expanded the bureaucracy by 4,000 public servants. Also the cost to industry of this tax in the first year alone, according to a report by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, was $9.5 billion. It cost the private sector $3 billion to implement the new tax and $6.6 billion for compliance within the first year.
In the last 12 months that the CFIB has studied the tax it has shown that the cost to our private sector for just collecting and remitting this tax and keeping the records was well over $4 billion at a time when that tax collected only $15 billion or $3 billion less than the MST it replaced.

May 11, 1993
Let us compare the 25 per cent or greater compliance cost to business with similar taxes we have seen. In Germany the cost to business of compliance with its VAT, value added tax, is 0.4 per cent and not over 25 per cent. In the U.K. the cost of compliance is 3.2 per cent.
The Tories have argued that because other countries had a VAT we should have the GST, except they failed to tell people one thing. It may be okay for Europe but our biggest trading partner that takes 80 per cent of our exports, the United States, does not have a value added tax.
What have we seen? We have seen tremendous growth in cross-border shopping. There has been a tax-driven flight from Canada so Canadians can purchase their goods in the United States. There has been absolute shock when American tourists come to Canada to purchase things or go to a restaurant and find they have to add the PST, GST and then a tip on top of that. Ask any border community that has been devastated what the costs have been in terms of lost revenue and jobs.
That was the stupidity of not looking at the competitive realities vis-a-vis the United States. We end up being the only country in the world that has two tax systems at the retail level: the provincial and the federal. European countries have only one tax at the retail level. The costs of administering this provincially are indeed high.
What is happening? We see more cross-border shopping and a burgeoning underground economy. Canadians do not want to be tax evaders but they have just said: "Enough is enough". Many transactions take place by cash or by barter and escape the net. That is what is going to happen when one hits the ceiling in taxation. People who are normally law-abiding Canadian citizens and want to be just feel they can no longer comply.
Also this tax is extremely difficult for small business to administer as opposed to bigger business. Bigger business has in-house accountants and lawyers who, with a little extra work, can handle the paperwork. Small businesses do not have that luxury. They had to go outside and hire accountants and lawyers and pay for them in order to undertake compliance with this tax.
Government Orders
Therefore I cannot think of a worse tax. The GST has to go. However, we are not going to, as the Tories did, impose a tax on Canadians or the provinces without consulting. It is critical for getting the costs of compliance down to integrate this tax with provincial needs and respond to their needs as well because we cannot afford a double bureaucracy to collect retail taxes. That is why it is critical that we have the time to consult with the provinces.
We saw the study by the C.D. Howe Institute a few days ago that said that our federation can no longer withstand the strains of the federal government dumping its deficit-cutting measures onto the provinces by reducing transfer payments. This is cutting the ability of the provinces to fund medicare, education and welfare. The welfare situation is caused by the mismanagement of our economy by our federal government.
This is why the only sane approach to replacing the GST is to ensure that we involve Canadians in the process by explaining to them what the needs are and letting them buy into a program of co-operative federalism involving the provinces whereby we can get the tax burdens or the burdens of compliance of the GST down to acceptable levels.
What else has this government done? It says that it has been able to deal with unemployment insurance. In the past the federal government usually paid about 30 per cent of the cost of unemployment insurance but this government-

speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.
I wonder if my hon. friend is aware that the bill before the House is Bill C-89, which is amendments to the Investment Canada Act. It is not a bill about the GST. It is not a bill about unemployment insurance. It is about Investment Canada about which I know my hon. friend has a great deal of expertise. I would appreciate an opportunity of hearing his comments on Bill C-89 which is I believe what is before the House right now.

Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to consider Bill C-89 without considering it within the context of the entire needs of Canada's economy. I will come back to Bill C-89 and this government's abortive policies regarding foreign investment in Canada, but part of what has gone wrong is not just a single issue but a mishmash of

May 11, 1993
Government Orders
Tory economic mismanagement. Therefore it is critical that we put it in the context that even my friend I hope will understand. I can understand why he is sensitive about these attacks.
It privatized unemployment insurance. This means now that employers pay about 60 per cent of it and the employees pay about 40 per cent of it. It is just an added tax to the private sector. It promised when it privatized unemployment insurance that it would not increase the burden that the private sector had to pay for the fees. It broke that promise twice.
Here is another thing that has gone wrong. I am sure my hon. friend the parliamentary secretary will want to know this. When this government took office in 1984, research and development in Canada was at the level of 1.41 per cent of our gross domestic product. Today it is at 1.37 per cent of GDP. It has actually fallen in spite of the promise of the Prime Minister that during his first four years in office he would double R and D.
Why did he promise that? It was because he knew that all our major competitors have levels of research and development that are at least twice the level of Canada's. His intentions were good, as so many of the intentions of this government were, but they have failed miserably. Our R and D is going down rather than going up.
Trade is another aspect of what this government has been all about in terms of its economic program. It felt that all we had to do was to introduce freer trade agreements and bring them into effect so they would immediately spill over their benefits to Canadians. We have seen how the deindustrialization of Canada has taken place at more than twice the rate of that of the United States.
There are a number of lessons that spring to us. I believe that we have learned or should have learned these during our more than four years since we have been dealing with the free trade issue. These are important because we are on the eve of entering into another agreement involving Mexico and the United States. I would hope that first of all we have learned in the last four years under free trade that Canada's abundant natural resources do not of themselves assure Canadians a high standard of living. We are going to
have to do better in the knowledge-based value-added manufacturing sectors.
Second, surely we have learned that we should not enter into a new free trade deal without having detailed impact assessments and specific adjustment programs in place. The government should come clean on where we are going to lose more jobs and what measures we can undertake to assist those workers. Also, perhaps if some industries are going to benefit, what can we do to maximize those benefits? Surely that is just sound planning.
Third, we have learned that a free trade agreement does not necessarily mean secure access to our foreign trading partner. Since this agreement with the United States was entered into we have had a spate of trade disagreements and an unprecedented level of trade harassment by the United States. But the Tories say: "It is wonderful that we have a dispute settlement mechanism". My God, we have a dispute settlement mechanism but it will be two years before the softwood issue will be ultimately resolved.
We have no supplementary agreement or side deal in the NAFTA dealing with environmental standards so that Canadian workers do not have to compete against people who can pollute to any extent they want. We want a side agreement on labour standards as do the Americans. The Americans want that side agreement on labour standards so that Mexican working conditions, child labour, salaries of only $1 U.S. an hour and conditions of plants can be brought up so that it does not create unfair competition for American workers.
Canadians should be insisting on a supplementary agreement dealing with the labour standards not only in Mexico but in the United States. In 20 states in the U.S. the minimum wage is $4 U.S. an hour or less. In six states there is no minimum wage. In 20 states they have right to work laws that have made it impossible for unions to respect the collective rights of workers. Those are the working conditions we are going to be competing with in the southern United States.
Why are we not insisting on a side deal for labour standards that would elevate the low U.S. standards that we would never tolerate here in our country? Instead, are we just going to say that the world should unfold as it
May 11, 1993

should as we lose more and more jobs south of the border?
Fourth, surely we have learned that U.S. trade harassment has a chilling effect on Canada's economy. Who is going to invest here if, for example, they can bring actions against our steel industry for dumping or for subsidies and effectively stop Canadians from selling to the U.S. market where we have been so successful and were successful before the FTA. There is no subsidies code in the NAFTA. There is no anti-dumping code. This government will not make it a condition or a precondition of enacting the NAFTA bill that we have a steel pact.
It is little wonder that Dofasco faced with all of these problems sets up its new mini-mill in the United States rather than in Canada. That is what is happening. The new investment to service the North American economy is not coming to Canada in the measure that it should because U.S. trade harassment can deny nine-tenths of the North American market to a Canadian manufacturer. That could be fixed up with a decent trade deal.
Fifth, as I mentioned earlier, when international rationalization does take place it is the Canadian branch plants that get closed down and not the American head offices. More than 50 per cent of our manufacturing sector in Canada is foreign owned. Most of it is in the States.
Sixth, we have learned the hard way that trade does not take place in a public policy vacuum and we have learned that when the dollar went from 76 cents to 90 cents-a 25 per cent hike in the value of the dollar- under the Tories' monetary policy that that was a greater disincentive to Canadians exporting to the United States than any of the U.S. tariff barriers that the trade deal might have removed. After all they stood at about only 2.5 per cent on a very small percentage of our products before the free trade agreement was brought in. This government had to pursue a monetary policy that was driving up the dollar and the value to make it almost impossible for us to compete.
Finally, and most important, I hope we have learned that trade policy is only one of the many elements of any economic strategy and not the major driving force.
Over the past nine years this government has been obsessed more with whom we trade with than what we
Government Orders
trade with. None of their policies conduce us to have a strong base that is necessary to allow us to take advantage of enhanced trade opportunities.
Lest one thinks the Liberals have their heads in the sand, we are the party of free trade. We are the party that over the decades has supported freer trade but also we have not supported unfair trade deals, uncompleted trade deals or trade deals that did not produce a level playing field for Canadians. But regardless of whether we have a free trade deal or not, Canadians have to compete. Regardless of whether NAFTA or the FTA are in place, we must still compete. Therefore, our onus will always be to become more productive on a global basis. This is where this government's policies have done just the opposite.
First of all, its tax policies have been high. Its monetary policy has driven up the value of the dollar. Its monetary policy has made our interest rates much higher than our competitors in the United States. Research and development was actually cut back. It has imposed new taxes and burdens on the private sector, including the unemployment insurance which it promised it would not increase.
It did not bring in adjustment programs. It has not put in place the type of teams that can go into a place like Scarborough when a GM plant closes down. The mandate of Investment Canada is to promote investment in Canada by Canadians and non-Canadians, to undertake research and provide policy advice on matters relating to investment and to review major foreign investments to determine if they are likely to be of net benefit for Canada.
Over the years the term "benefit for Canada" has gone from reviewing significant benefit for Canada to

It is time once again, because this debate comes before the House and before Canada from time to time, to discuss the issue of the amount of foreign ownership that is acceptable to Canadians. I do not think anyone should chastise Canadians for saying we are fearful about being too foreign dominated or too foreign controlled in our industrial and business sector. It should give all Canadians concern. I am sure that government members would also be concerned if we became too foreign dominated.
Just how involved is foreign investment in Canada? I wish to cite a few statistics that are now dated but nevertheless they were prevalent from 1985 to 1990. I suspect the statistics show even larger numbers at the present time, meaning that Investment Canada is not something to disregard and we cannot suggest that the bill has no consequence whatsoever.
From 1985 to June 1990 a total of 3,374 Canadian companies with assets of $81 billion were taken over by foreigners. Only 853 of those takeovers, representing 89 per cent of those foreign takeover assets, meaning $72 billion, were ever reviewed to determine net benefits to Canada and none of them were denied.
I spoke to a gentleman who was extremely helpful today, Mr. Caskey in the review division. Mr. Speaker, I propose in the next 10 minutes to deal with one very small element of the bill. I read clause 3 in its entirety. I quote: "Paragraph 14.1(8)(a) of the said act is repealed".
That is it, Mr. Speaker. No indication in that wording of what it is that is being repealed. The act, of course, is identified as the Investment Canada Act so we must go to the Investment Canada Act to find out what it is we are repealing.
What we find is the sections introduced in the act in 1988 in consequence of the negotiation of the free trade agreement with the United States. It took the limits for investment review that had been in the act and changed them, not for everybody, just for American investors. What for everybody else would automatically trigger a review by Investment Canada if an investment was proposed in excess of $5 million, for American investors that limit is now about $152 million. For a category of investment for anybody else which would trigger a review at $50 million, that category of investment is no longer reviewed at all for American investors.
That still leaves us wondering what exactly we are dealing with in 14.1(8)(a). So, flipping through the Investment Canada Act we find this section and it reads, and this is (8):
This section does not apply in respect of an investment to acquire control of a Canadian business that (a) engages in the development or production of oil or natural gas and owns an interest in proven reserves of oil or natural gas in Canada.
That meant that the special, much more generous review thresholds for Americans generally incorporated into the act were not incorporated for the purpose of oil and gas. For the purpose of oil and gas the older, more restrictive review thresholds still applied. They still applied as well for the mining and production of uranium, for any financial service, for any transportation service and for any cultural business.
What the act before us today, Bill C-89, purports to do in that innocuous teeny little clause 3 is remove those lower review thresholds for oil and gas.
This is actually the third of a three part policy that has been sought by this government to remove virtually all controls on foreign investment and ownership in the Canadian oil and gas industry. It started on March 25 of last year with the minister's announcement that the previous policy restricting foreign ownership in the Canadian oil and gas industry outside the Canada lands was no longer in effect. That policy was ditched. Henceforth, the sky was the limit for foreign ownership in oil and gas companies outside the Canada lands.
This was followed by Bill C-106, which most people expect will receive second reading tomorrow, which removes exactly the same ownership restrictions with regard to the Canada lands. With the passage of Bill C-106 no longer will there be Canadian ownership requirements in the Canada lands. Bill C-89 in its innocuous little clause numbered three is the third of the three horses in this particularly odious troika that is riding cheerfully over the frontiers of Canada's oil and gas industry, indeed Canada's strategic interest in its oil and gas industry, strategic interest that this government has systematically squandered.
Why has it done so? I would direct you to the U.S. president at that time, Mr. Reagan's message transmitted to Congress on July 25 of 1988 in a document entitled "Statement of Administrative Action". This

Mr. Speaker, I see that the clock will probably mean that I will not get through all of my remarks, but I will begin.
This whole notion of foreign investment has to be reviewed. I think of the very first bill that this government put in place when it became a government was Bill C-115, Investment Canada, Canada open for business. Quite frankly at that time I was supportive of the fact that we do a streamlining of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. The way the Investment Canada operation has unfolded is not working. Before I deal with the specifics of the bill I want to go back to the Foreign Investment Review Agency that was so popular under the Trudeau administration.
Canadians should understand that this was an agency of government that reviewed any investment that came to Canada. One of the great features of the Foreign Investment Review Agency was its ability to suggest to investors that we did not just want their money in this country; we wanted them to invest in a manufacturing operation. If they were coming to this country to do business in terms of sales or products we also wanted them to invest some money in research and development. I think of all the resistance we had over the years to the Foreign Investment Review Agency but 95 per cent to 96 per cent of the people who went through the Foreign Investment Review Agency were ultimately approved.
I can think of one example in particular. I remember in 1981-1982 Mercedes-Benz of Canada, the car dealer, wanted to expand its operations and sell more Mercedes-Benz cars in Canada. In order to have greater access to the Canadian market it had to go through the Foreign Investment Review Agency or FIRA. It told Mercedes-Benz of Canada, a division of Daimler-Benz of Germany, that it was welcome to sell its product in
Government Orders
Canada but at the same time it had to put something back into the country in terms of its ability to market and manufacture a world-class competitive product.
At that time there was a company in western Canada in Vancouver called Freightliner. Freightliner was on its hands and knees and was about to be closed down. Freightliner Canada was a division of the Freightliner organization based in Oregon and it wanted to bring its manufacturing plant back to the United States. The Foreign Investment Review Agency said it would not let Freightliner do that. If it wanted to sell more products in Canada, more Mercedes-Benz, then it had to commit to keeping Freightliner's manufacturing capability going in Canada.
I remember there were months and months of arguing with the Mercedes-Benz Corporation in Canada and I was directly involved. In the end the Mercedes-Benz approval begrudgingly went through but it also committed to keeping Freightliner as a manufacturing concern in Canada.
Freightliner, which at that time employed roughly 200 people now employs over 600 people in a brand new plant in St. Thomas, Ontario which was opened about a year ago.
Before I joined this debate today I spoke on the telephone with one of the senior executives of Freightliner who said business is booming. It has a full order book, is manufacturing the product and things are in good shape. This is a direct result not of the new approach to investment in Canada that this government is talking about but of the Trudeau approach to foreign investment where he told Mercedes-Benz if it wanted to sell its product in Canada it would have to keep that Freightliner manufacturing plant in Canada. It was not going to let it fold up shop in B.C. and go south to Oregon.
That is the difference. We, as Liberals, in a very respectful way would stand up to these transnational corporations and say: "If you want to sell your product in Canada, if you want to sell your merchandise in Canada, then we want you to make some products in Canada". Within six months we are going to go back to that policy and I will continue tomorrow.
