He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise to debate Bill C-396, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff with relation to child pornography. I think most Canadians would be surprised to learn that the possession of child pornography is not a criminal offence in Canada.
I have petitions from what looks like thousands of Canadians who are in support of this bill and in support of measures to curtail what is one of the most heinous of offences, that of maintaining a permanent record of a child being sexually abused. That is what child pornography is.
Each time someone taps into the pornographic underworld regarding children, the children are victimized over and over again. Bill C-396 would amend the Criminal Code to put an end to this cycle of child sexual abuse. This bill has six aspects and I will go through each one.
First of all, the bill provides a definition of child pornography. It proposes that the definition of the term child pornography contained in this bill indicates that pornography relating to children takes place where a child is used in pornographic performances or where somebody who appears to be or is depicted as being under the age of 18 is used in the production of pornographic materials.
Any pornographic material in which a child or someone who appears to be, or is depicted as being under the age of 18 would constitute child pornography.
The bill also creates new offences concerning the possession of child pornography, dealing in child pornography and using children in pornographic performances. The offences relating to pornography in Canada are presently covered under a very broad umbrella of obscenity legislation. This bill proposes that child pornography be dealt with specifically and separately. This legislation introduces a new crime, that of the possession of child pornography.
The bill also sets out rules for some of the defences available for these offences. If the communication or performance which is being discussed has artistic merit or is of an educational, scientific or medical purpose that would be a defence to the crime of possessing or dealing in child pornography.
The bill would also add child pornography to the list of prohibited goods for the purposes of the customs tariff to make it illegal to import or attempt to import child pornography specifically.
The bill provides for parliamentary review every five years so any technological developments affecting the production and dissemination of child pornography can be reviewed and the legislation amended accordingly.
This is particularly important because of the growth and advance of technology which now makes the dissemination of all materials, including child pornography, vety much simpler than it has ever been in the past. It is possible to take a video tape in one country, translate it from one computer to another and get a video tape at the other end. The transmission of child pornography is now very difficult to detect. Consequently, it is very important that we keep track of new technological developments.
Anyone found guilty of possession of child pornography under Bill C-396 would serve no more than two years in jail. A person guilty of dealing in child pornography under this bill would be liable to serve not more than 10 years for a first offence, not less than one or more than 10 for a second offence and not less than two or more than 10 for a third or any subsequent offence.
May 11, 1993

The purpose of the bill is to be clear about what child pornography is; to make possession of dealing in child pornography and use of children in pornographic performances a specific crime and to ensure that child pornography can be stopped or confiscated at the border.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River, the hon. member for Trinity- Spadina as well as the hon. member for Surrey North who seconded the bill. They, as well as others in the House, have indicated support for this legislation.
I would also call attention to the House the work of the hon. member opposite for Kitchener who has also put forward a private member's bill dealing with pornography.
If we canvassed the House we would find almost unanimous support for Bill C-396. However the bill was not deemed votable by the Private Members' Committee. In spite of that many people wrote to the committee and the chair of that committee seeking to ensure that the bill would be votable because of the widespread support for this measure across Canada.
It is worth remembering that in 1988 the Minister of Justice at that time, who also happened to be the hon. member of Parliament for the area I now represent, introduced broad based legislation dealing with obscenity and pornography. He included in that legislation provisions dealing with child pornography which received the general support of the House, those involved in policing pornographic materials and the public at large.
That was an omnibus piece of legislation which did not go on to be enacted but from 1988 the government opposite has indicated its commitment to dealing with this problem. Subsequently the Minister of Justice, now the Minister of National Defence, indicated her intention to introduce very soon, and this was some time in 1991, legislation dealing with child pornography. She did not do that and to date there has been no initiative from the Government of Canada dealing with what I think we all agree is something we really need to deal with in this country.
The present Minister of Justice has indicated that he does intend to introduce legislation dealing with child pornography, although as we all know we are veiy late in this parliamentary term and that would appear to be
Private Members' Business
more politics than an earnest desire to get this issue dealt with in legislation. If the members opposite had wanted to move this matter along, they could have ensured that Bill C-396, the bill we are debating today, was made votable.
I wish to draw attention to the support this bill has. As I have mentioned the 1988 legislation from the government included child pornography.
In June 1990 the special adviser to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in one of his recommendations called for the introduction of legislation "to address the protection of children from the harmful effects of pornography including a revision of the Criminal Code, harsher penalties for using children in the production of sexually explicit materials, and stricter monitoring of our borders by Customs and Excise officials. The processing of enacting legislation dealing with issues related to children and child pornography should be separated from that dealing with adults". As I say, there has not been any initiative in this House from the Government of Canada since that time.
The Fraser committee recommended revision of obscenity laws in 1985 and also was specific about child pornography. The Badgley committee in 1984 reported that domestically produced child pornography existed in an "informal and fragmented" system of private production and recommended that it be dealt with.
The head of Canada's only anti-pornography police squad, Detective Staff Sergeant Bob Matthews of the Ontario Provincial Police, has indicated that an average of 400 pieces of child pornography have been intercepted at border crossings in Canada each year over the past five years and I think we have to assume that there are many other pieces not found by customs officials and also many which are transmitted through electronic devices as I have mentioned.
The Conservative Party's family caucus has also recommended that the Criminal Code be changed to include specific reference to the use of children in a sexual manner, in other words in a special provision dealing with child pornography. I have received hundreds of thousands of signatures and dozens of phone calls in support of the legislation from all across

May 11, 1993
Private Members' Business
the country. I think it is clear that most Canadians support this initiative.
In closing this list of support, it is also the case that in signing the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child the Prime Minister on behalf of Canada committed "to take all appropriate legislative, administrative, social and educational measures to protect the child from all forms of physical or mental violence, injury or abuse, neglect and negligent treatment, maltreatment or exploitation including sexual abuse while in the care of parents, legal guardians or any other person who has the care of the child".
Canada has made an international commitment to the world that it would deal with this issue of child pornography. The government has yet to move in this area.
During the preparation of this bill I was lucky to have the earnest efforts of the staff of the House of Commons and also the support of Detective Staff Sergeant Bob Matthews, the head of Project P, Canada's only full-time anti-pornography squad, who has spoken often and strongly in favour of this piece of legislation.
I think we are all familiar with the subject. While most of us have not been exposed to this subject matter we know how damaging sexual abuse of children is and how long ranging the effects and the impact of that sexual abuse can be. We also know that it is an important and persistent problem in our society and we know that child pornography reflects and in fact distributes the visual effects of that child's sexual abuse.
I think all of us in the House would agree that we need to ensure that the distribution, possession and trading of child pornography should be stopped. In fact I suspect that if I ask for unanimous consent of the House to have this bill deemed votable that I might get it. I do not know if I could test the mood of the House in that regard. Do I have unanimous consent?
No.

Again we have members of the government not supporting proper measures to deal with child pornography, something which I think is most unfortunate.
In conclusion, I think it is only a matter of time before public pressure to deal with child pornography is enough to persuade even the government that some action is necessary. I look forward to that day. I thank all those who have indicated their support for this bill. I look forward to seeing the thrust of this bill, that is the creation of a criminal offence for the possession, trading and distribution of child pornography, introduced into the Criminal Code in the not too distant future.
Any initiative by the government or by any other member of Parliament to that effect would certainly receive my support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware the subject of pornography is one that has been of concern to many Canadians. It has been studied by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which came out with a report in 1978. The Badgley committee in 1984 and the Fraser committee in 1985 studied issues related to pornography and made recommendations as to how our laws might be changed to address this problem. Particular recommendations were made with respect to child pornography.
In the last 15 years, particularly the last nine years of which I am aware, the federal government has made two attempts to change the law with respect to pornography, including child pornography. The most recent bill was Bill C-54. It generated a considerable amount of controversy. It was one to this day I feel very badly about. It was the second attempt by the government to update Canada's pornography laws. Both bills died on the Order Paper.
What happens in this. As I say it is one of the disappointing things. Many groups say: "Yes, please do something about pornography. Pornography is vicious. Pornography is degrading to women. Pornography hurts people". Many individuals and groups say that but as soon as you put a definition on pornography then there are no shortages of critics who say: "Ah well, we are against pornography but you did not get it right. There are problems with your definition of pornography and of course we cannot support that". On the debate it somewhat degenerates and in the end somebody is
May 11, 1993

saying: "Well the government is trying to ban the Bible". That could be captured within this definition. So it was a very difficult one.
If any members want to talk to the hon. member for Kitchener, he too was quite interested in both those pieces of legislation. The people who wanted to see us do something in the area of pornography were very quiet. In fact the silence among people who were willing to give the government a hand was deafening. Of course the individuals on most pieces of legislation say: "Well nice try but you did not get it right". They of course were in full force on both those pieces of legislation.
As I say, for me it was one of the few disappointing initiatives of the 33rd Parliament that something in the area of pornography did not get put through. I thought the definitions were pretty good, but unless you come down from the mountain and these things are on tablets it is pretty difficult to get people to give you a break and support them.
The Supreme Court of Canada rendered its decision just this last year in the case of Regina and Butler. It upheld the current definition of obscenity. In the Butler decision, Mr. Justice Sopinka, writing for seven members of the court, referred to Bill C-54 which died on the Order Paper. I think his comments concerning the difficulty in trying to draft a piece of legislation in the area of pornography are good.
With respect to the attempt here by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing I am not going to be like all the critics in this area and try and start to take apart the bill. I am tempted to go through and say where I think it could be improved, but suffice it to say that I agree with the hon. member.
It was not long ago that the member for Edmonton- Strathcona, who has been very interested in seeing that something is done in the area of child pornography, was talking to me and other of his colleagues about bringing forth a piece of legislation to deal with this area. I personally would not have minded seeing something broader in the area but I think we should go with what we can get.
Certainly we have had guidelines in the Butler decision as to what would withstand a charter challenge. I think there is a consensus among most Canadians that
Private Members' Business
child pornography is abhorrent, that it is vicious and exploitive. It is the kind of thing that Canadian society will not tolerate.
The hon. member is impatient, he wants to see it. I can tell you, there has been no shortage of initiatives from the Department of Justice. I think he and most members would be aware that from the Department of Justice there has been a steady stream of good legislation, legislation that helps Canadians and legislation worthy of the support of Canadians.
In the wire-tap legislation the only part of it that seemed to get a lot of publicity was the part about cellular telephones. This is a very important instrument in the hands of police who are trying to control another aspect of crime, the area of drug investigations. We have that sort of thing. We have the proceeds of crime bill before Parliament. There are a number of them.
I take exception to any suggestion that the Department of Justice has not been working very diligently because other than finance, there is no other government department that has put more initiatives before this Parliament or indeed the last Parliament than the Department of Justice.
I can say to the hon. member that he is going to see government legislation in the area of child pornography. It will be specific. I think it will be a little more focused than the hon. member's private member's initiative, and I think he and other members of this House will be quite pleased. I can tell him that he will see that legislation very soon.
We have indicated this government's intention to bring forward child pornography legislation. I ask the hon. member to be patient just a little bit longer. He will see that legislation very soon. I hope, and I take him at his word, that it will have his support. We need that support.
I will tell him why. They are pretty sharp at the Department of Justice, but not perfect. No piece of legislation is perfect. On this we will need people's help. I have no doubt there will be no shortage of critics who will say we did not get it right or it is not perfect or we did not get this, that or the other thing. However time is short in the 34th Parliament. We will need the help of hon. members who will say: "Yes, this is a pretty good attempt. This gets at what we find abhorrent in Canadian society". It did not come down from the mountain on tablets. It came from the Department of Justice. They are pretty sharp. They do a good job. They have got a lot

May 11, 1993
Private Members' Business
of good legislation introduced by the minister and the previous minister before Parliament right now.
As I say I think he will see very soon government legislation specifically focusing in the area of child pornography. I call on all hon. members to get behind that government initiative and see that it becomes the law of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to express my support for Bill C-396, introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing.

This is a crime and justice issue as far as I am concerned and therefore I am delighted to be able to support it.
Just briefly, Bill C-396 would prevent the repetitive victimization of children by limiting the importation of pornographic material and imposing harsh penalties against the offender.
I think it is time that something was done and I commend my colleague for having taken this initiative. Perhaps it will at the same time give some impetus to the government to act on this particular issue.
I should point out that this bill is in keeping with article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and is in keeping with society's condemnation of child abuse generally.
In the crime and justice package my party proposed almost 10 days ago amendments to the Criminal Code would make it a crime to produce, sell, import, or possess child pornography. The promised reform was never acted upon by the Conservative government but we hear it may in fact happen very soon.
I want to add as well that Bill C-396 would amend the Criminal Code and Customs Tariff to eliminate protection from obscenity legislation. I think that is a step forward. Offenders could now be charged if found in possession of pornographic material.
Child pornography is in the same category as all other pornography. Implementation of this bill would facilitate the prosecution of known or suspected paedophiles.
I want very briefly to refer to the crime and justice package that the Liberal Party under our leader, helped by colleagues such as the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and the hon. member for Moncton proposed a short while ago.

We proposed a number of policies under the heading "Crime and Justice" reflecting Liberal views on the subject. I will only mention the headings but I think this should be of interest to many Canadians: "The battle against crime and for urban safety" is one subject that was considered in depth. Another one is "juvenile delinquents". We feel it is time to take a different and more serious approach to this group.
We also talked about gun control, a subject that has been widely discussed across Canada and on which action is really necessary. There was also prostitution and under that theme we talked about the rehabilitation of sex offenders. We also discussed violence against women and children, a terrible thing in our society that must be corrected.
We have also taken a position on forfeited property, sentence determination and social reintegration in the case of persons involved in various crimes. We also talked about conditional release, another burning issue in this countiy. I will get back to pornography later on when I will have a few things to say about it as one of the subjects included in the paper.
I would like to emphasize that my party intends to reinstate the Court Challenges Program and the Law Reform Commission because we feel the program and the commission had a vital role to play in our society.
Finally we have a section on so-called hate crimes. I would advise members of all parties to look at this policy paper which was released a short time ago.

With respect to pornography and that particular issue we have proposed amendments to the Criminal Code so that it would be a crime to produce, sell, import, or
May 11, 1993

possess child pornography, a reform that was promised but never acted upon by the Conservative government.
I want to share with my colleagues a section within this particular package on pornography that I think is useful. I quote from that document:
Pornography has been with us throughout history, and while there
have almost always been some restrictions placed on it, current
concerns stem from its increased availability, explicitness and a
growing awareness of the link to violence against women.
The principal existing sanction against pornography is found in the criminal law. Section 163 of the code makes it illegal to fabricate and distribute obscene publications or to possess them for the purpose of distribution. This law with its emphasis on sexual explicitness is seen by many as inadequate.
It should be noted that in North America pornography has exploded from a $5 million industry in the early 1970s to a $10 billion business today. That is a monumental growth and clearly one that has to be looked at very seriously.
Of the 10 most profitable magazines on the market today, six are "men's entertainment" magazines such as Playboy and Penthouse, outselling Time and Maclean's. Thirty per cent of all Canadian news-stand sales now consist of pornographic magazines. I find this statistic quite alarming.
Today many scholars and writers on the issue of pornography would like to see a differentiation made between pornography and erotica with the former being sanctioned against legislatively and the latter remaining legal.
Pornography could be defined as material designed to sexually stimulate the consumer by showing or describing a power imbalance among participants. This stimulates by showing or describing violence against or the degradation of a human being. Erotica could be defined as non-violent, non-degrading sexual material which also seeks to sexually stimulate the consumer, but not by depicting a power imbalance among participants.
These two definitions seem to be generally supported by the Supreme Court's recent ruling in the Butler case. Mr. Justice Sopinka held that existing sanctions against pornography, even in a society which protects free speech, are acceptable because of the harms which may
Private Members' Business
flow from such material to society and to women in particular. This case is particularly important in its recognition of the harm that pornography can cause.
Justice Sopinka said that while a direct link between obscenity and harm to society may never be conclusively established, there is sufficient evidence of harm to justify laws which restrict pornography. He noted as well that if true equality between men and women is to be achieved, we cannot ignore the threat to equality resulting from violent and degrading material. Justice Sopinka thus concluded that legislation describing obscenity has a valid objective that justifies some encroachment on the right to freedom of speech.
The Butler case has opened the door for legislation prohibiting violent and very degrading pornography and to regulate the display and location of sale of materials which, while pornographic, are neither violent nor very degrading.
Let me terminate my remarks by saying I am particularly pleased that members of Parliament would in fact address this exceptionally important issue. I am delighted that my colleague from Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing has taken this initiative. I am exceptionally pleased that my party has come forward with a crime and justice package that addresses several issues which I have mentioned, including the issue of pornography. I am hoping that these various initiatives will encourage the government to go forward.

It is time to move ahead. The matter has been debated often and at length, but it is now time to act.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words tonight about this private member's bill, Bill C-396, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff in consequence thereof.
I want to use the few minutes I have to point out the things I think are extremely noteworthy in the bill, to point out some of the concerns in the area of child pornography and some of the actions and inactions of the Government of Canada and, if I may say so, some of the concerns that I would have specifically with the bill we are discussing today.

May 11, 1993
Private Members' Business
First of all, it is important for people watching to understand that it is currently not a crime in this country to possess child pornography for personal use. That is completely legal. Most people would not believe this. Most people would not believe that it is absolutely legal to possess depictions of children, photographs of children in sexually compromised situations and that there is absolutely nothing we can do about it.
Why is this important? This is crucially important because the only people who are interested in the possession of child pornography are paedophiles. I would also say it is true that there are very few passive paedophiles, if I can put it that way, those who are prepared to go no further than to look at pictures.
We also know from various studies that paedophiles prey on children. There are no one-victim paedophiles. In fact most of the studies that have been done show that paedophiles, both heterosexual and homosexual, prey on more than 200 children each in their lifetimes.
Who are we benefiting by not making child pornography illegal? Paedophiles are the people who are interested in looking at young children, children as young as infants, involved in sexual acts.
Why do I say this? I say it because we should not even be discussing a bill like this. That situation should not even be allowed to be the law of Canada at the present time. In my view that is the direct responsibility of the Government of Canada.
Nine years ago this issue was not one that was talked about. We did not know too much about it. The information that we now have was really hidden. Over the course of nine years it has become clear that child sexual abuse is far more rampant in our society than we ever thought it was or would be.
What has happened? Nothing. It is still quite legal to possess child pornography in this country provided that the person does not want to sell it. What are we talking about? Let us say we are talking about a photograph or a video. What is that? That is the capturing on film of the sexual exploitation of children. That is what it is. Every photograph, every video shows the victimization of a child.
We also know from people like Detective Sergeant Bob Matthews from Project P in the Ontario Provincial Police that many pieces of child pornography are amateur. What does that mean? That means that these paedophiles lure our Canadian children into situations where they take photographs or videos of them and then use those photographs or videos of our Canadian children for their own pleasure. What is more, they trade them. They cannot sell them because selling any sort of pornography is illegal. However they can trade one type of video or one type of photograph or series of photographs with other paedophiles.
How would they know about other paedophiles? There are groups of people who get together as paedophiles, proudly I might say, and say that they are paedophiles and that there is absolutely nothing wrong with this. One of those groups is the North American Man-Boy Love Association which advocates absolutely no age of consent law whatsoever so that even our youngest infants would be subject to sexual exploitation by paedophiles.
That group and its aims are perfectly legal at the present time. What kind of a country do we have if we do not protect our children from paedophiles? What has our government done about it? It has done absolutely nothing.
In the dying days of a Parliament we are told by the Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice that lo and behold the government has suddenly discovered this issue and it is going to bring forth something that it thinks we will like. How horribly cynical it is that after nine years of inaction it has all of a sudden discovered sexual exploitation of children and is going to do something about it.
One of the problems was, and the government was told more than once, that it should not lump all pornography together. Let us deal strictly with child pornography. It did not listen. Now all of a sudden it sees the error of its ways.
One of the things I like about this bill is that it recognizes that child pornography is wrong, that it is not a victimless crime. Every child depicted is a victim for life. They are scarred forever and those are the people we have to protect in this country.
The bill proposes to make the possession of child pornography illegal. I applaud the hon. member for that
May 11, 1993

sentiment. He also does something which is interesting. When we hear lawyers talking, and I am one too, we talk about all kinds of technical details. He deals with one, which is what is a child? He says, and many would disagree but I agree with him, that for this purpose a child is anyone under the age of 18 years.
He also provides what I would consider to be reasonable deterrent penalties for the possession of child pornography, not Draconian but reasonable penalties to deter people from owning and possessing child pornography.
One of the problems I have with the bill is the attempt to define child pornography. In my view it is far too specific. Whenever we try to define something we end up leaving out so many other things.
I would have preferred to see a far more broadly based definition such as any video picture or written description which in any way advocates the sexual exploitation of children and let the courts decide based on the evidence in front of them whether or not there is the advocating or actual sexual exploitation of children.
The member goes through very specific details but my concern is, and this is a legal matter, if we set out very specific details in legislation and the case does not fall within those very specific details then there is no crime. That is a problem.
I do not say that in a negative sense to the hon. member, but I do say to the government that in whatever bill it has suddenly discovered is on the legislative agenda it should provide for the broadest possible spectrum of what could be defined as child pornography because I would rather err on the side of protecting child victims than on the side of protecting child paedophiles.
I commend the hon. member for recognizing a problem which the government has failed to recognize and for at least having the initiative to bring it to the House so we can talk about it. I, for one, am not prepared to let the government off the hook.
Private Members' Business
It is important for the people of Canada to know that at this very moment as we speak anyone can possess child pornography in this country. That in itself is a crime.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start off by commending the member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing for his perseverance in bringing this particular private members' bill to the floor.
I also want to say that I am rather annoyed but not surprised that there was not unanimous consent to have this as a votable item. People who watch us, either from the gallery or at home on television, wonder how in the name of goodness we ever get our business done. They wonder how we priorize our activities in this place. I guess even members who have been here a lot longer than I sometimes question those priorities as well.
Surely if there is one thing we are sent here to do it is to try to make this place that we live in, Canada, a more decent place to live. Surely if there is one thing that we are sent here to do it is to try to pass legislation and set the parameters of morality by our regulations and our actions here. Most important, we have a special responsibility to those individuals who are not able to look after themselves, be they the old and the infirm, the sick, those who are economically disadvantaged or our children, our most precious resource as parents, members of communities, and Canadians.
They are our future but they are defenceless. When they come into this world they would not be able to survive for a few hours if it were not for the love, comfort and caring that a parent and a mother brings. As they grow up they develop almost on a daily basis and find new things to do and new joys to give their parents.
As a parent I will tell you that one of the things that strikes fear in my heart is the possibility that one of my children, either the nine-year-old, the six-year-old and one just a little under two-years-old, would become the victim of a sexual assault. It scares the life out of me because I do not know how I would cope with it. I certainly do not know how a child could recover from it.
A lot of times when we are debating people's rights and who has the right to do this, that or the other thing,

May 11, 1993
Private Members' Business
surely members on all sides must understand that we owe our children the utmost degree of protection from exploitation in any form but most particularly sexual exploitation.
This bill brings forward the whole subject of child pornography, child abuse and sexual exploitation of our children by individuals that I guess can be described in some pretty miserable terms, but certainly individuals who are not well balanced. Anybody that would abuse a child physically or sexually cannot have it together. Rather than strike out at those individuals harshly, perhaps we should try to deal with their problems. But most of all, we have to protect our children.
Bill C-396 seeks to do that. If this bill were a votable motion and was enacted by this Parliament, it would make it illegal for people to possess child pornography. My colleague behind me just spoke about that. Think about it. It may be illegal to sell it but we have clubs, as we have just heard, of paedophiles with amateur photographs of our children perhaps and it is not illegal for them to trade them. It is like a book of the month club of exploitation of our most precious resource and the most vulnerable in our society, our children.
The bill seeks to impose penalties on those that would possess child pornography. I am not a lawyer and I do not know what would be an appropriate penalty, but two years in prison for possession of child pornography somehow does not seem like very much to me, knowing how our criminal justice system works and knowing that they would not see two years. It would only be a number of months before they would be out.
For the production and sale of child pornography, five years. I know that we are supposed to have a Christian heart and we are supposed to look at rehabilitation. Somehow if it were my child, I would find it very difficult that somebody who had taken advantage of my children in that situation would, if they got the maximum sentence, be out in probably about one-third of their sentence.
Rather than deal with the problem after it happens why is it that this is not a priority? Back in my riding of Dartmouth we are dealing with a community and personal tragedies on a daily basis. We have children in our community, juveniles under the age of 18 who have been the victims of pimps. Everybody has read about it right across the country in the newspapers.
True low-lifes, bottom dwellers, scum who take advantage of young girls and young boys, but mostly young girls in our community, who suck them in at 11, 12, 13. Imagine, at 11 years of age. The task force on prostitution told me 11 years of age. That is a child. They cannot make up their minds whether to go to McDonald's or Pizza Hut for supper and they were forced and pushed into prostitution and drug abuse by low-lifes because they need the bucks. The dollar is more important to the pimp than anything else.
A lot of these girls who were lured into prostitution, hooked on drugs and exploited were also exploited for the purposes of child pornography. Even when they are taken out of that situation and rehabilitation is tried, they do not know that there is not a man down the street who has a picture of them in a compromising position from when they were exploited by their pimp. They live in fear for the rest of their lives that that type of publication is there.
Children that have been exploited physically, mentally, emotionally but most of all sexually, have been scarred for life. It is not a matter that the day after they say: "It has all been done, the person has been put in jail, I can go on and lead my life". It does not happen that way. That is convenient. Would it not be easy if we could compartmentalize those types of traumas in our lives? The psychiatric wards would not be filled up in hospitals right across this country with abused adults or adults that were abused as children.
Most of us here have children. If we do not have them ourselves we have grandsons or granddaughters or nephews or nieces. This should be a priority for us. We are dealing with assault on our children in the school yards. I was at a meeting in Dartmouth last night-that is why I was not here yesterday-of concerned parents. They are concerned about the rising escalation of violence against their children in their schools: five, six, seven, eight, ten, twelve-year olds who are being victimized by older students. They are concerned and trying to figure out ways to grapple with it. About 150 people showed up last night.
We are legislators. We are parliamentarians. We are the ones that can make the laws that can make a difference. When this motion came up before, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing sought unanimous consent to make it a votable motion. I am trying not to make this a partisan issue, but I am not the person

that puts bills on the Order Paper. It is the government. It is the people opposite. It has to be priorized.
It is said that this came in the dying days of this session of this Parliament. Everybody knows in another 10 days or two weeks there is not going to be another Parliament. There will be an election. No wonder there is cynicism by people out there at the priorization action by the Parliament of Canada.
I hope that this type of initiative from the member from Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing will be applauded by all members. I hope individuals who are out there watching, and I know there are some people who do watch what we do here, would write to their member of Parliament and say this is exactly the type of action that must be taken. The bill may be imperfect, but it is going in the right direction.
I would say to the member that I want to thank him for bringing this to the attention of the House. If government members opposite are truly interested in stopping this type of abuse, they should bring a bill before this Parliament. I for one on this side will support and try to expedite the passage of that legislation so our children are no longer at risk of sexual exploitation.

Mr. Speaker, on April 28, 1993 I put a question to the right hon. Prime Minister and the response came from the Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons. It was with regard to the issue of Somalia and what was taking place there. Specifically I was talking about the board of inquiry which the Minister of National Defence announced would investigate some of the allegations of events that had taken place.
Part of our thesis at that time was that the board of inquiry ought not to be held in secrecy but that it ought to open itself to public hearings so that many individuals

May 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
would have the opportunity to express themselves with regard to the serious issues of the day.
In point of fact I asked the government House leader:
-the minister knows very well that there are many unanswered questions still to be discussed.and answers to be provided.
For instance, why did the senior military commander in Somalia try to conceal one of the four deaths as the minister claimed? Why was the minister not told it was homicide for two weeks, so the minister claims?
Now General MacKenzie-said: "I am very concerned for the morale of our troops in Somalia".
The inquiry announced by the minister of defence is being held from the point of view of a person who had to find some way to deflect or to delay.
I want the House to understand that many of us on the opposition benches are extremely supportive and have been for many years of the Canadian Armed Forces. We hold in high regard the distinguished, reputable careers and reputations of the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces, but we do not believe it is in their best interests or in the best interests of Canada that the minister responsible for the Department of National Defence hold an inquiry in secret.
Having an inquiry behind closed doors will not adduce the kind of evidence and the kind of testimony which will be important for Canadians to see and to understand. I hope the parliamentary secretary who will be answering on behalf of the minister here tonight will see that what we are asking is both reasonable and appropriate.
The board of inquiry should be made public. It should open itself to testimony from a variety of sources so that we can have full accountability of the minister's role as to what is taking place in the Canadian Armed Forces.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary opposite, who is a reasonable and distinguished individual and happens to be with the Government of Canada at the present time, would accept my submission as being reasonable and objective. It would be in the best interest not only of the Canadian Armed Forces but indeed all of Canada to have this kind of evidence and testimony presented in an open public forum as opposed to behind closed doors in secret where no individual has the opportunity to question or raise doubt in terms of the efficacy of that particular testimony.
I would ask that the parliamentary secretary give careful consideration to this very reasonable request. I think it is warranted and certainly Canadians need to have all the facts as to what has taken place in that situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take the next few minutes to answer some of the points brought by the member from Cape Breton-East Richmond. I hope that my comments will help him understand the situation and will clarify the whole affair.
As we know there has been a great deal of uninformed comments on four recent events in Somalia. There have been suggestions that incidents have been covered up and that investigations are proceeding in secrecy. Concern has also been expressed about the suitability of the Canadian forces unit sent to Somalia.
I would like to put to rest first the notion that there has been any kind of cover-up or whitewash. Each of the four events has been or is being investigated. In each case the Canadian forces gave public notice of the incident. The details are on public record and are summarized in the minister's statement in the House on April 26, 1993.
Departmental communication policy was adhered to in all cases. When weaknesses in this policy became evident the minister acted quickly to improve departmental procedure to ensure that it worked effectively.
I would like to comment on the board of inquiry on the Canadian Airborne Regiment battle group which has been convened by the chief of defence staff at the minister's request.
The board of inquiry is to examine whether any of the concerns arising from the Canadian forces operation in Somalia are the result of systemic problems, particularly in the Airborne Regiment. More specifically this board of inquiry is tasked with the broad mandate of investigating the leadership, discipline, operation, actions and procedure of the Canadian Airborne Regiment battle group.

Mr. Speaker, in 1965 our government realized that Canadian magazine publishers did not have a level playing field or an equal opportunity to compete with their American counterparts.
They felt that it was very important to have in Canada an indigenous magazine publishing industry, so-called cultural industries which are necessary in order to reinforce what it is to be Canadian. What happened is our government took measures to ensure that the Americans could not compete unfairly.
One of the ways they were competing unfairly was very simple. With their big markets south of the border, they were able to do all of the editorial work, the writing, all the staff work on a magazine. Then they could ship it into Canada without any changes, soak up Canadian advertising revenues and take that money out of Canada. This made it very difficult for Canadian magazines to compete.
A number of steps were undertaken, including tariff items, which would have precluded this dumping of U.S. editorial content into the Canadian market. We are saying if you are a foreign magazine and you want to come into Canada you must act like a Canadian magazine. You must have your writing here, your editorial staff here, your support staff. In other words act the same way a Canadian magazine does if you want the benefits of being in Canada.
Through high-priced lawyers, Time Warner in the United States which publishes Sports Illustrated found a loophole. Under our tariff rules if you do not have the Canadian content requirements our tariff officials could stop you at the border and preclude that shipment of magazines from entering Canada. They found a loophole. What they do is prepare the magazine entirely in the United States, or almost entirely. Then they electronically ship it into Canada right into a printing shop so that it gets printed here. Through technological means they are able to get around the spirit and intent of our 1965 laws.
This has serious implications for Canadian magazine publishers. There are many foreign magazines which are now waiting to see what this government's reaction will
Adjournment Debate
be so that they can take advantage of sopping up Canadian advertising dollars for their magazines but putting very little into Canada itself. There are a number of jobs, over 6,000, that are at stake, but what is more important is what is at stake is our cultural future.
When confronted with this loophole which it has known about since last fall, the government said it would not act. It would not go to Time Warner and tell them it could not bring Sports Illustrated in this way. It said it would let them bring it in and see what it looks like. It would not presume.
That is not the way it acted with a number of other publications. This was a special favour it gave to Sports Illustrated. Why? What were the personal connections that this government had that made Sports Illustrated special?

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments may take more than four minutes, but since I have only two minutes, I will accelerate.
The Minister of Communications has asked me to thank the hon. member for Willowdale for the opportunity to confirm this government's commitment to policies that create a positive environment for the growth of a strong Canadian-owned magazine industry that contributes to our cultural and economic development.
To be more precise, let me answer directly the hon. member's question: Will the Minister say no to Sports Illustrated and to all other foreign publishers that seek to violate Canada's laws and to ruin Canada's magazine industry?
For more than 25 years the government has strengthened the Canadian magazine industry through legislation designed to maintain advertising revenues in Canada through direct support from the Canada Council and through the postal subsidy.
The legislation and policies which have been in place since 1965 are intended to ensure Canadian's continued access to as wide a range of Canadian magazines as possible. The government's measures which have contributed to the development of the Canadian magazine industry include Code 9958 of the Customs Thriff. This measure prohibits the importation into Canada of subsequent issues of a magazine in which the advertishing

May 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
content was directed at the Canadian market. This measure remains in force.
In addition, section 19 of the Income Tax Act disallows a deduction for advertising expenditures in non-Canadian magazines where the advertising is directed primarily at a market in Canada.
This government recognizes that Canadian magazines are an important medium of cultural expression among Canadians and that access to Canadian advertising dollars is vital to maintaining a healthy Canadian periodical industry.
In the Sports Illustrated case, I understand that Revenue Canada has determined that the Canadian edition of this magazine does not contravene tariff 9958 because it is printed in Canada.
Should foreign publishers decide, during the work of this task force, to undertake any new publishing activity in Canada which would contravene or sidestep the government's policy objectives for the magazine industry, they would be doing so at their own risk.

Mr. Speaker, if I could take 15 seconds to digress just a bit from the appropriate question I am going to ask, I would like to suggest that the Memorial Cup is in Sault Ste. Marie this year. The Sault Ste. Marie Junior Greyhounds are in the Memorial Cup for the third consecutive year. I invite all of Canada to Sault Ste. Marie. Now I will get to the issue, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate the latitude you allowed me.
The P.E.I. link question is a disaster no matter how you slice it: How not to propose a study; how not to propose financing for a small project, let alone a megaproject. It has been an absolute chaotic nightmare for all of those involved.
I want to say that this bridge proposal was privately driven. No government said: "We need to have a tunnel or a bridge or whatever between Prince Edward Island
and Nova Scotia or New Brunswick". It was private industry that said: "We want to build this".
I would hope that people would be altruistic and say that they want to build it to benefit the Islanders. The way it has unfolded has been a source of controversy and a source of more studies. I am told by the minister that they would reach the very ceiling of this House of Commons.
The studies go on but the final definitive study that should have been tabled by the Government of Canada has not yet been tabled despite the fact that study after study suggested that we require a full environmental assessment before we can proceed. We have financial problems with it. There are some mathematical problems. It is perhaps not economical. We kind of sense that the ice flow is going to create serious damage for the scallop industry. It is going to put hundreds of people out of work.
All these were brought forward and yet the government proceeded. Now we are long down the road and we have not yet had the final definitive study.
The Federal Court said: "No, you must have this full environmental review". Very very quickly the proponents came up with an environmental evaluation of SCI's proposed Northumberland Strait crossing project. That I believe was put together in a couple of weeks' time.
It was suggested today by my colleague from British Columbia that it is the taxpayers who are going to foot the bill for this. Yes, we are going to inherit a bridge 35 years from now but should anything happen in the interim who will be responsible? It will be the taxpayer.
The bottom line is that all of the opposition that I spoke to at committee said that if there is an environmental review, a full environmental assessment, and it comes out positively, they will support the link.
Hindsight is easy but I am sure had the government known that it would have conducted that full environmental review, its own review process it should have followed, could have followed and must have followed. Now it is faced with a major dilemma, going against its own experts suggesting a year and a half ago-but, no, this was not good enough-a generic study. A generic study was done. Of course, a generic study does not foot
May 11, 1993

the bill when you have an actual proposal in front of the government.
To complete my question, why is the government going forward with this proposal when it knows know there are environmental concerns and financial concerns? Why does it continue the way it is? Why not do the full environmental assessment? If it proves positive everybody in Canada will be pleased and accept this link.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that most people in Canada are and should be excited about the fixed link project.
First off, it was a project initiated by the maritime provinces in Atlantic Canada. They are not only very interested in this project but they feel it is crucial to the long-term viability and economic well-being of the people of Prince Edward Island.
If the hon. member was really concerned about the taxpayers across the country, he would see that they will end up far better off over the long term.
I feel very comfortable that this project is in the best interest of my constituents in British Columbia as well as the people from Atlantic Canada.
In the last seven years since the idea of the construction of a fixed link from Borden to Cape Tormentine has come up, the federal government has insisted that the matter proceed with care and thoroughness and that all processes, legal and otherwise, be respected. No short cuts have been taken, but as the hon. member has indicated, there have been many reviews. In fact, there have been over 64 public meetings.
The department is currently conducting another review as directed by the federal court. In conjunction with that, there have been four more public meetings, two in Prince Edward Island, one in Nova Scotia and another in New Brunswick.
The department is going to be recommending to the minister very shortly based on the input the department has received: the written information that has been sent in, the 1-800 information that has come in, the over 90 studies that had already been conducted and the 64 public meetings that have been held.
Adjournment Debate INDIAN AFFAIRS

Mr. Speaker, I want to discuss a subject that involves implicit fiduciary responsibility on behalf of the federal government with respect to contract works on native reservations and the matter of financial responsibility for the administration of the funding and payment of those contracts.
In many cases, particularly where there is a dispute in the contract, there is a predicament for contractors or suppliers to exercise financial judgments on native reservations because of provisions of the Indian Act which prevent the seizing of real property or real assets to satisfy a judgment.
In the case of a contract dispute, for example, irrespective of who is at fault, the native administration is in a position to arbitrarily withhold payment. Even though the contractor is able to seek and obtain a judgment, he is not able to exercise that judgment so in the final analysis he has no legal or financial recourse.
On those projects on native reservations that are funded by the federal government, there is perceived by many business citizens of Canada to be a significant moral and fiduciary responsibility on the part of the federal government to ensure that those funds flow in such a way that contractors are assured of payment before final hold-backs are released as is the manner in normal contract provisions outside native reservations.
Will the government consider introducing a process for publicly-funded projects on native reservations that does conform to the contract law and the financial funding provisions that are normally applicable under Canadian contract construction administration? Will the government accept a fiduciary responsibility to ensure the payment of those contracts and the protection of the interests of both non-native contractors and natives, depending upon how the dispute is resolved in future contract work on native reservations?
I think there is a very significant implicit responsibility on the part of the federal government. There is a manner through the hold-back process, the contractor approval process and the funding approval process where the interests of all parties can be protected, even in the cases of matters in dispute, where funds can be placed in escrow while the dispute is being resolved.
The question is, where public funds are involved will the federal government accept a fiduciary and financial

May 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
responsibility to ensure that the financial obligations of the contract are fulfilled?

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fredericton-York-Sunbury has expressed a very legitimate concern in regard to the policy of the department in situations where suppliers or contractors are experiencing difficulty in collecting outstanding accounts from Indian bands.
Since the 1970s the federal government has been transferring responsibility for the delivery of community services to Indian bands. This has been done to break a legacy of dependency.
In 1993-94 First Nations will manage 78 per cent of the funds directed to community services. This amounts to approximately $2.5 billion. It will involve many thousands of agreements between Indian councils, suppliers and contractors. It will involve a broad range of goods and services.
I view this as a very important issue that must be dealt with responsibly and effectively. However these are agreements between private parties and for their mutual benefit. The department is not a party to these transactions. With any transaction there are risks and the parties to the agreement must weigh these risks as they would with any other commercial undertaking.
As Indian bands assume management of their affairs they develop more effective business relationships. They realize the importance of these relationships to securing quality goods and services at a reasonable cost. This is a fundamental step on the path to self-sufficiency.
The department encourages First Nations to develop and maintain effective business relationships. It encourages sound financial management as well as accountability. However it does not intervene in agreements freely entered into between two private parties. The issue is really one of accountability and it must be to the local level of government.
